4818: The Five-Limbed Ritual Manual (Pañcāṅga) of the Nine-Syllable Caṇḍī, from the Rudrayāmala.

Oṃ caṃ paṃ. Folio 1a. Oṃ, salutations to the venerable Guru, the Auspicious One (Śiva). Oṃ, I shall now describe the chapter on the nine-syllabled mantra, which bestows all desired objects; when employed according to its own specific rules in the six applications such as subjugation (*vaśya*) and others, it always grants one's wishes. [The extraction of the mantra...]
I perform the worship of the nine-syllable mantra, by the mere knowledge of which wisdom is bestowed upon men: *oṃ* is the first seed-syllable, possessing a luster equal to the moon;
*hrīṃ* is the second, radiant with the brilliance of the sun; and *klīṃ*.
The third [face] has a form equal to that of a Vaiśya woman; the fourth is inconceivable, with an infinite mouth and the luster of a pure-born [being];
the fifth is fashioned as exceedingly red; and the sixth is fierce, removing all afflictions.
The seventh is red in nature, very black, and a slayer of enemies;
the eighth is white, beginningless, and perfected by Tvaṣṭṛ; the ninth is smoke-colored and vast. Thus, the vowels are of nine syllables, having the form of the color *kila*.

Because she bestows the bliss of liberation and other benefits, the mantra Mahālakṣmī is established in this nine-syllabled [mantra]. Therefore, she is self-perfected for all and a lamp in every direction; such is the nine-syllabled Ṛk.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the six [deities];
the meters declared by the sages are Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, and Anuṣṭubh; the goddesses declared are Mahāpūrvā, Kālī, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Nandā, Śākaṃbharī, and Bhīmā.

The powers (śaktis) of this mantra are Mā, Śakti, Asya, Manoḥ, Mattā, Syāt, Raktadantikā, Durgā, Bhrāmari, and the collection of seeds (bījas). Agni, Vāyu, Bhaga, Tat-tvam, and the fruit arising from the three Vedas are for the sake of accomplishing all desired objects.

The application (viniyoga) has been declared; one should place the seer (ṛṣi), meter (chandas), and deity upon the head, mouth, and heart. Having placed the seed-syllables of the Śaktis upon the breasts, one should again place them in the heart. Thereafter, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga).
One should perform the ritual with the mantras divided according to their root-syllables—individually, one by one, four by four, or as a whole—at the house of the mendicant.
Having performed the rite of placement (*nyāsa*) thus, she is emanated: *Oṃ Caṃ Paṃ Daṃ Gāni Ṣaṃ Mukhī*. Thus, having completed the procedure of placement, she is created.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa). Now I shall describe the yantra that bestows all accomplishments:
one should draw an eight-petalled lotus and a hexagon, O Caṇḍikā, joined with anklets and the Trailokyavijayā [mantra].

One should place the three primordial seed-syllables situated in the center of the six-cornered wheel (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*). Among them, first, Mahālakṣmī is established in the central seed-syllable; Mahākālī is in the right, and Sarasvatī is in the left.
One should place the other seed-syllables in the six triangles starting from the east; then, having worshipped the *ādhāra* and the others, one should subsequently place the *jayā* and others.
Then, recollecting the seat with the mantra "Obeisance to the Māyā-lotus-seat" (*māyādipadmāsanāya namaḥ*), [one should worship] the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
Then, for the sake of worship, he sprinkles the substances starting from the nine seeds;
he should establish the *arghya* there, having displayed the *dhenu-yoni* [mudrā],
and then having formed the *mīna-mudrā*, he should cover the root [mantra] and mutter it eight times.
Having invoked the eight *dhātī-tīrthas* and offered the ritual substances,
one should then form the *mīna-mudrā*, bow down to the root of the *śrāddha*, and [again] invoke the eight *dhātī-tīrthas* and offer the ritual substances.
"One should meditate separately upon Thava, Kṣema, Īśāni, Dhyāna, Khaḍga, Cakra, Gada, and Iṣu. Thus, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, the meditation of Mahākālī has been described;
now I shall declare the meditation of Mahālakṣmī.
Having meditated thus upon "naṃ sarva-samṛddhi-da akṣa-sṛk-paraśu," one should always meditate on the Great Vāṇī,
O Ambikā; [and] "ghaṃṭā-śūla" is the mantra of Mahākālī.

The sage is Padmabhū standing firm; the meter is the joyful Gāyatrī; the deity is Mahākālī; the seed-syllable is Vāk (Aiṃ); the element is Fire; the application is for the sake of Dharma and Artha; thus has it been declared for the middle [finger].
Thereafter, the third Great Goddess is Uṣṇik-chandas-Mahālakṣmī;
her seed-syllable is *oṃ caṃ paṃ*, she is sealed by the Vāyu-tattva, and her application is declared to be for the attainment of wealth. Regarding the third Great Goddess, the Ṛk... [pṛ0 3a]

The seed-syllable (bīja) is "Ṣiḥ," the deity is Sarasvatī preceded by Mahā, the meter (chandas) is Triṣṭubh, and the element (tattva) is Ravi; its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of desire.
Now, I shall describe the worship of the letter 'A' at the conclusion [of the ritual].

In brief, one should worship the first seat as Oṃkārapīṭha, then Pūrṇapīṭha, and thirdly Kāmapīṭha, according to the tradition; and in the directions starting from the east, one should worship the four [deities] beginning with Gaṇeśa at the seat.
One should worship Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Ācāryapādukā, and Vaṭuka—the triad—in the four directions beginning with the southeast (Agni), as well as the four goddesses:
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā; thus [are] the goddesses.
Having performed worship, one should then worship Sarasvatī on the petal at the middle corner, as well as Padmaja (Brahmā), Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, Umā, and Mahādeva,
in order from the east, [starting] with the one situated in the center.

One should first worship Mahālakṣmī with the seed-syllable; to her right, Mahākālī, and to her left, Mahāsarasvatī. One should worship the Supreme Goddess with special offerings on the right side of the Goddess.
One should worship Bhāgeśvarī in the [western] portion; then, having worshipped Siṃha in the north, one should worship the six Śaktis within the hexagon: Nandajā, Raktadantā, Śākambharī, and Durgā.
One should worship [the goddess] beginning with "Thā-bhī-mā-bhra-marī-ce-ti" followed by the six vowels with the bindu (Ṃ),
having the color of wine, and ending with "Namaḥ," in each of the corners; thereafter, the Mothers should be worshipped, beginning with Brāhmī.
On the first lunar day (pratipad), one should worship, as previously described, the seven Śaktis: Īśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Aindrī as the seventh, and Cāmuṇḍā.
Oṃ Caṃ Paṃ. On the three filaments (p. 4a), the Śaktis are, in order: Viṣṇu, Māyā, and Cetanā; Vidhi, Nidrā, and Kṣudh; Chāyā-Śakti, Tṛṣṇā, Kṣānti, Jāti, and likewise Lajjā.

Śānti, Aśraddhā, Kānti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Vṛti, Smṛti, Avṛṣṭi, Puṣṭi—after these Mothers, one should again speak of the twenty-four ending with Bhrānti and Vyāpti. Caturviṃ... [Caturviṃ] (The twenty-four).
One should worship [the deities] in sequence upon the sixty filaments (kesara), worshipping them as before with the syllable Om at the beginning and end.
At the base of the stalk (nāla), one should worship the four supports beginning with Ādhāra; these are Ādhāra and Kūrma.
In the remaining fourth [corner], O auspicious Earth, one should worship Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Vaṭuka, and likewise the Yoginī in the corners of the house;
outside, one should worship Indra and the others, and the weapons such as the thunderbolt (vajra) and so forth at the entrance.

One should worship that [deity] in the external sequence; then, having performed the great worship (mahatī-pūjā) and recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, one should dismiss the Goddess and bring her back into the heart. Having done thus, one should... [ja].

One should offer four hundred oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) into the fire while the golden deity is being worshipped; with a tenth part of that, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the deity,
with a tenth part of that, the sprinkling (mārjana), and with a tenth part of that...
O beloved, one should feed the Śena-Brahmins while performing the *puraścaryā*;
thus one should carry out the ritual applications. During the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, beginning from the first day (*pratipad*), having made them equal, [one should perform] nine...
A wise person should mutter this mantra that many times and worship it daily.
One should worship nine auspicious virgins (*kanyā*), beginning with those two years old and ending with those ten years old, in due order. First, one should worship the one-year-old girl...
O Supreme Goddess, the names of these [energies] in the sequence of the nose (nāsākrama), excluding the years beginning with Pabhāva, are now being told: the two-year-old is Cakrī;
she is joined with Oṃcaṃpa; Trimūrti is three years old; and Caturabdhā is four years old.
A five-year-old Rohiṇī is called Tukalyāṇī; a six-year-old is said to be Kānikā;
a seven-year-old is Caṇḍikā; an eight-year-old is Śāmbhavī;
a nine-year-old is Durgā; and a [ten-year-old] is Subhadrā.
One should worship with the mantras prescribed for each year; having propitiated her daily according to the specific year by these names, [one may encounter her] as one with deficient limbs,
or with extra limbs, or likewise afflicted by leprosy, ulcers, or blindness.
A maiden who is not ugly, not squinting, and not having reddish-brown eyes—

such as one born of a slave-girl or a sister-in-law— and who is avoided [by others], should be taken from a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of success in one's endeavors; one born of a Kṣatriya brings fame, while one born of a Vaiśya brings wealth.

For the sake of obtaining a husband and for the attainment of sons, one should sacrifice to a Śūdra-born woman on an auspicious maṇḍala drawn upon an altar or similar surface; having duly established a water-pot there and invoked the Goddess Śivā, one should worship her, and before her, [worship] a maiden.
One should also worship the Brahmins with various services and offerings for the castes and classes. In the autumn season,
during the month of Āśvina, in the bright fortnight, one should begin on the first lunar day (pratipad) for the Great Goddess (Maheśvarī).

One should complete [the rite] ending with the vomiting [of the poison], and then offer oblations (*bali*) to the gods in the sequence beginning from the east, using perfumes, flowers, clarified butter, incense, lamps,
and excellent unguents; I shall now state their names in brief.
O beloved, hear [of them]: Kādambarī is mounted upon an elephant; Punaruktā has the form of a lotus; Karālī is mounted upon a buffalo; Raktākṣī is stationed upon a preta;
Śvetā is matured upon a crocodile; Haritā has a deer as her vehicle; Yakṣiṇī is situated on the back of a lion; and Kaṅkālī is upon a bull.

One should worship the vehicles, such as the back of a swan for the eldest of the gods (Brahmā), and those devoted to me; one should also worship these deities, the nine planets, the world-protectors, and the guardians of the directions, as proclaimed by Pulastya.

One should worship all the gods and goddesses with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra). One should feed the Mārīs, the foremost Brāhmaṇas, and others according to the prescribed rites. On the first day, one should perform the worship of Caṇḍikā and other such ceremonies.
On the second day, one should perform twice that amount; on the following day, three times that.

One should offer worship, recitation (*japa*), and so forth, until the end of the lunar day (*tithi*). On a single day, the observer of the vow should perform it, endowed with restraints such as truthfulness and the like. Having performed [the rite],...
One should complete everything from the *tvāhoma* onwards up to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

Setting aside what is too extensive or elaborate, one should perform the recitation until the moon is satisfied. In that context, for the principal *homa*, the three sweets (*trimadhu*) are considered the best.
The sacrificial materials consist of rice, sesame seeds, and beans,
as well as bilva fruits, various kinds of divine fruits,
kiñcukas, mustard seeds, betel nuts, and likewise divine sprouts of dūrvā grass.

One should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) with *karavīra* flowers, red flowers, white and red lotuses, pieces of red sandalwood, and enchanting *guggulu*, using oil mixed with red sandalwood and black mustard seeds; [one should offer] a thousand [oblations]. (Homa-pṛ0 6ba)
By offering [the oblation] alone, one brings the king under control;
by offering honey and *śokapuṣpa* flowers for three nights as before, one becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) through the bestowal of the *Chandī-mantra* for the sake of wealth.

For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), one should offer *bilva* leaves; for the sake of sons, *karavīra* flowers and *japā* blossoms; and for the sake of contentment, having offered *tulasī* leaves and lotuses, one should fulfill all desires. For subjugation, meditation is said to be intensely red; for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), it is variegated; for eradication (*uccāṭana*)...
A smoky color and black are prescribed for killing; one desiring progeny should meditate on a shadow that is dark like a blue lotus. By meditating on a red [shadow], one shall attain all desires.
O Śivā, meditation on the battle-mantra is proclaimed as being like a forest fire that completely dries up the water;
and the moon, accompanied by a shower of nectar, is for one terrified by the fear of poison and the like.
Oṃ caṃ paṃ (pṛ0 7a). Through the yoga of supreme meditation, a person becomes fearless. Now I shall further explain the supreme sādhana of the nine syllables:
having consecrated the ground and established a flask with water from a sacred ford.
Having filled it, one should then cast eight types of earth into a golden vessel; one desiring merit should cast ashes, one desiring wealth should cast pearls,
one desiring prosperity should place a lotus, and for the sake of desire, one should place yellow orpiment.

One desiring liberation should wear *mokṣaka* cloth; one desiring success in recitation (*japa*), *aparājitā*; one seeking to drive away enemies, *vyāghrī*; one seeking subjugation (*vaśya*), the root of *śikhin*;
for killing (*māraṇa*), *marīca*; and for enchantment (*mohana*), *kaitaka*.

O Maheśānī, one should cast into the interior of the pitcher that which brings about attraction; listen as I speak the mantra to be recited. Having taken from the hand that which was cast into the pitcher, one should then recite the mantra. Do not...

One should utter the syllable *lī* struck by the left ear (*śa*), with the head of *indra* (*ra*) and the letter born of speech (*va*) twice; then one should speak the *māyā*-seed-syllable (*hrīṃ*). After that, the word *cāmuṇḍāyai* followed by the *dviṇṭha* (*svāhā*) is declared to be the mantra for recitation.
Having bathed with that very water for twelve kalpas, one should offer oblations of sesame, grains, and rice smeared with clarified butter;
for the complete attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa).
In the rites of killing and liberation, as well as in the rite of eradication, one should offer a *huṅkāra* oblation soaked in the three sweets (*trimadhu*).
For the rite of delusion, honey and milk-rice (*pāyasa*); for paralyzing, the fruit of the *mātuluṅga*; and for subjugation, white mustard seeds. Regarding Dharma...

One should perform the oblation facing the eastern direction for the sake of wealth, desire, and liberation; for the purpose of eradication (*uccāṭana*), one should face the northern direction—such is the established rule.
Now I shall further explain another mantra that bestows swift results. [The Veda...]

The seed-syllable of Divya, Māyā, and likewise Kāma; the Earth (la), the letter Ra, and the left eye (i), adorned with Nāda and Bindu; Māyā (hrīṃ), Kāma (klīṃ), Oṃ, Jvālā (svā), and Pa (pha)—after this, the Root Mantra is proclaimed. One should recite it one hundred thousand times (lakṣa).

For the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals, one should recite the root mantra one hundred times at the beginning and one hundred times at the end, as well as the nine-syllable mantra. This is declared to be the "Seal-Encasement" (*mudrā-sampuṭa*) for the *Caṇḍī-saptaśatī* when used by those possessing desires. It is [to be] encased...

For this hymn of seven hundred verses (*saptaśatī*), which is to be recited without the *niṣkāma-sampuṭa*, Medhātithi is said to be the seer (*ṛṣi*). The meters (*chandas*) are Gāyatrī, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī.
The syllables *va-tā-stve-va-kā-lī* are Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Mahā; the preceding cluster is the *stavaka*;
the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is known as *vāṅ-māyā-kāma*; thereafter is *nṛsiṃha*, proclaimed as the *śakti* and the *netra*. This is the fulfillment of all desires.
One should meditate upon her here and recite the mantra that has emerged;

then, O Beloved, having meditated on Caṇḍīmadhukai according to the previously stated sequence, one should constantly practice for the sake of attaining the desired success. Then, [one should perform] the *kā...* [rite].
pṛ0 8ba) One should protect [it]. Now, the nine-syllable Gāyatrī for Kātyāyanī:
"We know Kanyākumārī; may we meditate upon her;
may that Caṇḍī inspire us. Thus ends the Śrī-Vārā...
The ninth chapter on the *hataṃtra* (the severed mantra), concerning the ocean-like expanse, is complete.

Oṃ. Now the ritual worship (pūjā) is described. Oṃ. If one who is devoted to the Goddess should perform worship without having first performed the morning rites, her worship shall indeed be fruitless due to the lack of purification in the proper sequence. Oṃ. During the Brāhma-muhūrta...
Having risen from his bed, washed his hands and feet,
and sat upon his seat, [he visualized] within the pericarp of a thousand-petaled white lotus facing downward upon his own head...
And one should visualize one's own Guru seated upon a lunar disc in the sky,
white in color, adorned with white ornaments, his mind delighted by the bliss of primordial wisdom, his form consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and possessing three eyes.
Oṃ caṃ paṃ: [He is] four-armed, with hands holding the *jñānamudrā*, a book, a boon-granting gesture (*varada*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*);
his left side is embraced by his beloved with her right arm, she who holds a lotus in her left hand and wears red garments and ornaments. Sa...
Having meditated upon the Lord, whose nature is that of Supreme Śiva, who is quiescent and worshipped by all the gods,
and having visualized one's own self bathed by the stream of nectar flowing from His pair of lotus feet, one should worship Him with mental offerings.
Having contemplated the Śrī Guru-mantra ten times with the mind,
one should perform prostrations like a staff and practice prāṇāyāma, [reciting]: "Oṃ, I bow my head to the true Guru, the peaceful one, who is manifest in the form of Śiva, the seat of yoga."
For the sake of attaining the goals of stability, liberation, and desire, I bow to the glorious Guru, Supreme Bliss,
whose form is the bliss of knowledge; by whose mere presence the supreme, indivisible, and all-pervading sphere of consciousness-bliss arises.

Salutations to that venerable Guru by whom [the truth] was revealed, through whom the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded, and who is the Guru Brahmā, the Guru Viṣṇu, and the Guru Maheśvara himself; to him, the venerable Guru, salutations.
The Guru alone is the entire universe. To that venerable Guru... [end of fragment]

Obeisance to Rūva! Obeisance to you, O Lord, the Blessed Śiva, who exists in the form of the Guru; who has assumed manifold bodies for the sake of the perfect accomplishment of the descent of knowledge; who possesses ever-new forms, yet whose sole true nature is the Supreme Reality.
Salutations to the Supreme Self, who is like the sun that shatters the darkness of all ignorance; who is the dense mass of consciousness;
who is independent, yet whose form is fashioned for the sake of others; who is dependent upon those devoted and fortunate ones, appearing in the form of worldly existence for their sake.

To those who possess discernment, for the sake of discernment; to those who possess inquiry, for the sake of inquiry; to those who possess illumination, for the sake of illumination; to those who possess knowledge, to Him whose form is knowledge—to Him I bow with my head, touching His sides, above, and below.

Having prostrated to the venerable Guru with the thought, "The attainment of the disembodied state occurs through the form of the mind as a servant," and having meditated upon him as being well-pleased,
one should take his command from the mind with the syllables *oṃ caṃ paṃ*, and then [activate] Kuṇḍalinī by means of the sequence of ascending and descending.
One who has received the secret instruction (saṃketa) should meditate upon the venerable Guru according to the path taught by the venerable Guru, preceded by the sounding and fixing [of the breath],
and by some manifestation of consciousness in which all limiting adjuncts have been removed.

Having contemplated, "I am existing," and having offered one's own activity with the thought, "Whatever I do from morning until evening, and from evening until morning, O Source of the World, that is my worship of You," one should offer it.

For the performance of one’s own duty, having prayed to the Earth with: "Oṃ, O Goddess whose girdle is the ocean, whose breasts are the mountains, O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you; forgive this touch of my feet," [he should proceed] following his breath.

Having placed his feet upon that spot and come outside, he should go toward the southwest or the north direction, and having passed a distance of one *śara-kṣepa* (the range of an arrow-shot), he should there perform the evacuation of feces and urine,
purification, sipping water (*ācamana*), cleaning the teeth, and so forth.
Having rinsed the mouth with the root mantra (*mūla*), having gone out from the small room,

and having visualized everything in the form of the illustrious Caṇḍikā, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). Then, while recollecting the root mantra, one should perform the bath for the extraction of the root (*mūlākarṣana-snāna*) according to the Vedic bath prescribed in one's own Vedic school (*sva-śākhā*).

Having performed the *namaskāra* and sipped water (*ācamana*), one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Oṃ, on this day of such-and-such month, etc., for the sake of pleasing the venerable family deity (*kuladevatā*), I shall perform the Tantric bath. Then, [one should perform] breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and [recite the names of the] seers (*ṛṣi*).

Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) of the directions, one should draw a triangular wheel (*trikoṇacakra*) in the water before oneself; then, [reciting]: "By that truth, O Lord of Gods, through which the holy waters and other sanctuaries within the belly of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) were touched by Your hands, grant me these holy waters."

Having prayed to the Sūryatīrtha as "Divāṅkara," and having entered the solar orb with the *kuśa* mudrā while uttering "Krom," [one recites]: "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and indeed Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu..."
"O Kāverī, take up residence in this water"— with this solar mantra,
*oṃ caṃ paṃ*, having drawn the sacred water (*tīrtha*) from the *paṇḍala* and joined it with the previously prepared water,
one should stir it with *hrīṃ* and transform it into nectar (*amṛta*) by means of the *dhenu-mudrā* while reciting *vaṃ*.

Having performed the *tīkṛti* [ritual], one should place the three principles (*tattva*) in the water, reciting: "Oṃ, svāhā to the Self-principle (Ātmatattva)! [Mūla-mantra]; "Oṃ, svāhā to the Knowledge-principle (Vidyātattva)! [Mūla-mantra]; "Oṃ, svāhā to the Śiva-principle (Śivatattva)! [Mūla-mantra]. Therein, one should [visualize] the Śrīcakra.
Having visualized [the deity] in the water, having invoked the Goddess within the expanse of the heart-lotus,
and having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the six limbs, one should bathe her along with her retinue;
then, with the *yonimudrā*, one should empower that blazing [deity] eight times with the mantra.
Having first recollected the deity of the *tīrtha*, having immersed yourself three times and emerged,
sprinkle your own head three times with the root mantra using the *kumbha-mudrā*;
having thrice offered libations to the Goddess with the root mantra, [place] the Goddess within your own heart.
"Oṃ nīrya-mūlam ātma-tattvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā;
vidyā-tattvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā; śiva-tattvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā. Having thus sipped water three times, [he puts on] two garments.
Above the *ridhāyati* [mantra], with the mantra: *oṃ maṇidhari vajraṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa rakṣa huṃ phaṭ svāhā*,
one should bind the topknot (*śikhā*) and offer three *muṇḍa* heads upon the crown of the head with the root mantra.
Having performed the Vedic *saṃdhyā* and completed it, one should begin the Tantric rite; there,
having sipped water (*ācamana*) as before, preceded by *prāṇāyāma*,
the assignment of the seers (*ṛṣi*), and so forth, and the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), [one should meditate] upon one's own city in front.

Having likewise consecrated the water from a sacred site (tīrtha) with the *numudrā* and rendered it nectar (*amṛta*) by reciting the root mantra eight times, one should take water in the left hand, cover it with the right hand, and [recite] *haṃ yaṃ vaṃ laṃ raṃ*.
Having consecrated [the water] seven times with the root mantra and three times again,

one should sprinkle one’s own head three times with drops of that water using the *tattvamudrā* and the root mantra; then, placing the remaining water in the right hand, [one should contemplate] the light.
Oṃ caṃ paṃ (pṛ0 12a). Having drawn in with the *iḍā* [channel] the water at the end of form, which is black in color, one washes away all impurities situated within one's own body;
that black-colored water then exits outward through the *piṅgalā* [channel].
Having placed you in his left hand and visualized a diamond-stone (*vajraśilā*) on his own left side with old age, he strikes that stone with the *Paśupati-astra* mantra: *oṃ ślīṃ paśu huṃ phaṭ*.

Having washed both hands and taken water with the root mantra, one should visualize it as having become one with the supreme nectar of the thousand-petaled lotus within the flowing river; then, having brought it forth, [one should offer] that water to Mṛtamālinī.

Having sprinkled one's own head three times with "Svāhā," having sipped water as before and then sipping water in reverse order, and having sipped water three times with "Mūlaṃ sarvatattvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā," [one should recite] "Mūlaṃ" for the three seed-syllables.
We meditate upon that Śakti; may she inspire our intellect. Oṃ, this is the *argha* for the sandals of the venerable Cāmuṇḍā; svāhā!
Having thus offered the *argha* three times with the root mantra to the Goddess, [one recites]: Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ.

Having offered three *arghya* oblations to the Kula-Sūrya with the mantra "Mārtāṇḍabhairava-prakāśa-śakti-sahita eṣa te arghyaḥ svāhā," and having thrice gratified the Śrī Devī with the root mantra, [one should likewise gratify] the Śrī Guru and the Sun three times.

Having satiated [the deity] at the *mūlādhāra* and meditated upon the three primary seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the root mantra, one should invoke [the deity] into the fire-mandala situated in space; there,
having meditated upon the Goddess in the form of the auspicious twilight (*sandhyā*), [one should worship her] with the root *gāyatrī*.
Having offered *arghya* to the goddess Lajjā and having satisfied her thrice, one should bow to the venerable Guru.

Then, preceded by *prāṇāyāma* and other preliminary rites, one should recite the root mantra and the *Gāyatrī*; and in the morning, one should also recite the mantra of Vāgīśvarī and the root mantra as well.

Having recited [the mantra] as many times as possible and having offered the recitation along with the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and other rites to the Goddess, one should [visualize] the Root Goddess descending from the solar orb into the fire orb, together with the rays of light, in the form of the morning twilight, accompanied by her own seed-syllable (bīja).
Oṃ caṃ paṃ pṛ0 13a) [End of page 13a]. [Note: The text fragment "Oṃ caṃ paṃ" likely refers to specific seed-syllables or mantras associated with the visualization.]

Having released that [breath] from the *mūlādhāra*, one should bow to the venerable Guru; this is the procedure for the morning twilight (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyā*). Now follows the midday twilight (*madhyāhna-saṃdhyā*):
therein, at midday, the seed-syllable of the root-mantra (*mūla-vidyā*) is in the *anāhata-cakra*.

One should meditate on the two [discs] as red in color, possessing intense luster like fire. Having invoked [the deity] into the solar mandala, and having meditated there upon the Goddess Śrī in her youthful form,
one should offer the *arghya* to the Goddess Śrī with the previously mentioned root *gāyatrī*.

Having recited [the mantra] as much as one's ability permits with the root Gāyatrī, and having likewise recited the two secondary seed-syllables and the root [mantra] as much as one's ability permits,
one should offer the recitation through breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other means, and then prostrate.

Having projected the Mūladevī, who possesses a youthful form, into one's own heart, one should prostrate to the Śrī Guru; this is the midday *saṃdhyā*. Now, what is the evening *saṃdhyā*? In that regard, the procedure from *prāṇāyāma* up to the libation (*tarpaṇa*) to the Sun is to be performed as before.

(p. 13b) He who would perform the seed-sandhyā: there, at evening, having invoked the two root-seeds (mūlavīja), white in color, into the lunar maṇḍala situated in space, [he should worship] Śrī... there, in her mature form...

Having meditated upon the Goddess and offered *arghya* with the root *gāyatrī*, one should recite this root *gāyatrī* as many times as possible; then, having offered the recitation through *prāṇāyāma* and other means, [one should draw it] forth from the lunar orb (*somamaṇḍala*).

Having brought the form [of the deity] to the *ājñācakra* and the Root Goddess (*mūladevī*) to the heart, one should bow to the venerable Guru; this is the evening twilight ritual (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyā*). Then, having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites according to the Tantric tradition for the deities of the directions, one should perform the recollection (*smaraṇa*).
Then, rising up while recollecting the root mantra,
one should go to the house of Gaṅgā; having brought water with the left hand while reciting "Oṃ vajrodaki hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should sprinkle the place.
Having entered, recite: *oṃ hrīṃ viśuddha-sarva-pāpāni śama oṃ caṃ paṃ pṛ0 14a) yā-aśeṣa-vikalpaṃ apanaya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having thus washed one's own feet and sipped water (*ācamana*) as before, [proceed to] the door.

One should worship the respective deities with "Obeisance to the four castes according to their respective colors," "Aṃ Āṃ," and so forth, and "Obeisance to the one adorned by the nine divisions, the island consisting of the nine gems, [and] the Nandana garden."
*Yaṃ namaḥ* to the goldsmith; *namaḥ* twice. At the top and bottom of the right and left door-frames (*śikhā*) of that door: *4ṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ*;
*4ṃ kṣaṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ*. *3ṃ* at the door.
Having entered inside the door with water while reciting "śriyai 2 4ṃ daṃdehalyainamaḥ 2," one should worship there with "4ṃ kaṃkadamvakānanāya 2," "4ṃ śrī ratnamaṇḍapāya," and "4ṃ tatravārāhyai 2."
On the upper right branch of the door: 4ṃ Māṃ Mahālakṣmyai namaḥ. On the left: 4ṃ Sāṃ Sarasvatyai namaḥ. In the middle: 4ṃ Duṃ Durgāyai namaḥ. 4ṃ Dvāṃ Dvāraśriyai namaḥ. [End of] Door.

Below the right and left tufts of hair, [one should worship]: OṂ ŚAṂ ŚAṄKHANIDHIVASUDHĀBHYO NAMAḤ (OṂ ŚAṂ, obeisance to Śaṅkhanidhi and Vasudhā). OṂ GAṂ GAṆAPATAYE NAMAḤ (OṂ GAṂ, obeisance to Gaṇapati).
OṂ KṢAṂ KṢETRAPĀLĀYA NAMAḤ (OṂ KṢAṂ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla). OṂ MĀṂ MĀYĀŚAKTAYE NAMAḤ (OṂ MĀṂ, obeisance to Māyāśakti). OṂ CIṂ...
Oṃ śilakṣmyai namaḥ. 4ṃ Gaṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ. 4ṃ Yaṃ yamunāyai namaḥ.
4ṃ Dhaṃ dhātryai namaḥ. 4ṃ Viṃ vidhātryai namaḥ. 4ṃ Daṃ dehalyai namaḥ at the front of the door. 4ṃ Vaṃ varuṇāya.
Having worshipped the western door with *maḥ 4ṃ*, then at the northern door, having worshipped Mahālakṣmī and Sarasvatī as before, [one should worship] in the center:
*4ṃ vāṃ vaṭukāya namaḥ* and *dvāṃ dvārāśriyai namaḥ*. Pū.
Having worshipped from the threshold (śekha) up to the lintel (dehalī) with "Oṃ Saṃ Somāya Namaḥ" at the front of the door,
one should likewise worship Mahālakṣmī and the others at the eastern door, extending from Kṣetra up to the lintel.

Having worshipped [the deity] with *oṃ caṃ paṃ* at the front of the door (*pṛ0 15a*), one should worship Indra with *4ṃ laṃ indrāya namaḥ*. Then, at the southern door, having worshipped Mahālakṣmī and Sarasvatī as before, one should worship Gaṇanātha in the middle with *4ṃ glauṃ gaṇanāthāya namaḥ*. At the door...

Having worshipped [the deities] starting from the Śaṅkha-nidhi and ending at the threshold (dehalī) with "Oṃ Raśriyai Namaḥ" as before, one should worship in front of the door: "4ṃ Ṭaṃ Yamunāyai Namaḥ.
Then, again at the western door: "4ṃ Ratnasopānapaṅktaye Namaḥ."

Having ascended that [pedestal], one should worship the five deities at the four doors of the pavilion, beginning with the western door, as follows: *Oṃ namo bhagavati māheśvari paśujanamanaścakṣustiraskaraṇam*.

Having worshipped with "kuru 2 svāhā," [one should worship] slightly outside the front of the western door, at the front of that door, with: 4ṃ gauṃ gauriye namaḥ, 4ṃ lauṃ lokadhātryai namaḥ, 4ṃ vāṃ vāgīśvaryai namaḥ, 4ṃ.
Then, right there, I worship the divine lineage (divyaugha) Śrīpādukā;
*namaḥ*, I offer libation (*tarpaṇa*), *namaḥ* (four times). 4ṃ, the perfected lineage (siddhaugha) Śrīpādukā;
4ṃ, the human lineage (mānavaugha) Śrīpādukā. Beyond that—
At the door: 4ṃ Māṃmāya-śrīpādukāṃ. Then again, having worshipped Gaurī and the others, then at the eastern door: 4ṃ Bhaṃ Bhadrakālī-śrīpādukāṃ; 4ṃ Svaṃ Svasti-śrīpādukāṃ. Then...

As before, [worship] Gaurī and the others; then at the southern gate: 4ṃ Svāṃ Svā Hā Śrīpādukam, 4ṃ Śuṃ Śubhaṅkarī Śrīpādukam. As before, [worship] Gaurī and the others; then at the western gate: Pālitam.
Having meditated thus: "I take refuge in the great temple of Bhavānī at the western gate, which is adorned with supreme sovereignty by Hiriṃdra and others," one should say:
"Obeisance to the western gate and the jeweled pavilion."
Having worshipped the pavilion and ascended its door preceded by three claps of the hands, [one recites]:
*Oṃ nīlaṃ turaṅgam adhiruhya suśobhamānāṃ nīlāṃśuka-bharaṇa-mālya-vibhūṣaṇāḍhyā nidrā*.
"May the Goddess, who conceals the worlds with her garment and whose weapon is a sword,
protect us"— thus one should meditate upon Her.
If one is unable to perform this meditation, [one should worship] Gaṇeśa above the door.
Maḥ—obeisance to Vāṭuka on the right; Kṣāṃ—obeisance to Kṣetrapāla on the left; Yāṃ—obeisance to the Yoginīs below;
E—obeisance to Gaṅgā; Vaṃ—obeisance to Yamunā; Śrīṃ—obeisance to Lakṣmī.

Having worshipped the four directions beginning with the east with "Oṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī; salutation," one should then, by means of white mustard seeds, unbroken rice, and so forth, using the Nārāca-weapon yoga, [drive away] the wandering bhūtas, piśācas, pretas, and others.

O spirits who dwell here, and other deities established upon the earth, depart! Having become [invisible], those beings who are established on the ground— those spirits who create obstacles— may they perish through the power of Śiva.

Having recited the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) "jñayā," and having sprinkled water inside the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) with the mantra "oṃ sarvavighnānutsāraya huṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should [visualize] the obstacles that are departing as being on one's own left side.
"Having given the path to Kocena, let those who cause heresy on earth,
those who move in the atmosphere, and those who dwell in the heavenly world—
let them perish by the command of Śiva. At the end [of this], with the Astra-mantra, [he should strike] the left foot...

Having dispelled the terrestrial, atmospheric, and celestial obstacles by means of the three *ṛṣṇighātas*, the three *tālas*, and the divine gaze (*divyadṛṣṭi*), one should enter within the mandala preceded by the left foot;
thus concludes the worship of the door (*dvārapūjā*). Here, in this [context]...

If there is no door, one should worship after meditating upon all the doors as being in the west. There, having illuminated the pavilion and adorned it with garlands and other offerings, [one should offer] "Oṃ Vāstupuruṣāya Namaḥ" in the southwest (Nairṛta). Oṃ Vā...
Salutation to Brahmā, the Lord of the Self (Stvadhīśvara). In the Īśāna [direction]:
4ṃ Kulanā Oṃ Caṃ Paṃ Pṛ0 17a) Tha Śrīpādukāṃ. Having thus worshipped the Śrīpādukā of the twelve red-colored Śaktis, [one worships] with: 4ṃ Bhairava-Śrīpādukāṃ. Thus.
Having fully worshipped Bhairava and received his command, one goes to the sacrificial altar with the mantra *aḥ phaṭ*,
and then [protects] the ground of the vajra-pavitra with *oṃ rakṣa 2 huṃ phaṭ svāhā* and *ta taḥ pavitravajrabhūmau huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having consecrated the ground with water released from his clenched fist and performed the propitiation of the earth as prescribed, he established the seat,
drew a triangular mandala upon the ground, and [invoked] the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti) therein.
Having worshipped with "Oṃ namas," having established a seat of kuśa grass, and with palms joined in reverence, [one should recite]: "Oṃ, of this Śrī Āsana-śodhana mantra,
Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi), Sutala is the meter (chandas), and Kūrma is..."
Having remembered, "The viniyoga is for the purification of the seat by the deities," one should assign:
"Salutation to Merupṛṣṭha, the Ṛṣi, at the head; salutation to Supratiṣṭhita, the Chandas, in the mouth; salutation to Kūrma, the Devatā, in the heart."

Having thus arranged [the ritual], this is the application for requesting me to sit upon the seat. Having spoken with palms joined, and having offered three blades of *kuśa* grass upon the seat, he said: "O Earth, you who were supported by [Viṣṇu]..."
"O Earth, you were held by Viṣṇu; may you also hold me.

Make this seat pure. Having thus prayed to the Earth, one should perform *japa* at that place, gaze upon it with the root mantra (*mūla*), sprinkle it with the weapon mantra (*astra*), and likewise [protect] it with the weapon mantra.
Having sprinkled [the area] with water empowered by the *Śaistrisaṃtāḍyaka* armor-mantra,
and having worshipped from the *Ḍamuku-Kālāgnirudra* up to the altar according to the sequence for the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) to be described, [one worships] "Hrīṃ, Ādhāraśakti, Kamalā."

Having worshipped with "Oṃ namaḥ," and having formed the maṇḍala for the seat with "Aḥ surekhe vajrare khe huṃ phaṭ svāhā," [one should place] "Gaṃ" for Gaṇapati in the corners of the seat, beginning from the southeast.

Oṃ caṃ paṃ pṛ 18a) Homage to Durgā; homage to Sarasvatī; homage to Kṣetrapāla. Having thus worshipped, one should sit there upon a lotus-seat [and recite]: Oṃ, you who are consciousness, born of Brahman, daughter of Brahman.
O ever sinless one, for the sake of the satisfaction of the Brahmins, be pure now.
*Oṃ brāhmaṇyai namaḥ svāhā*. O Goddess who destroys the price of worldly success, you who awaken those of deficient understanding, [protect] the king and the subjects.

O destroyer of the wings of the enemy Śaṅkāri, Oṃ, obeisance and svāhā to the Kṣatriya! O you whose tip blazes with the fuel of ignorance, O fire of knowledge in the form of Brahman, accept this oblation of bliss and joy for the sake of perfect knowledge.

I offer salutations to you, Hrīṃ, the Vaiśya; I bow, I bow again to you, O Goddess who reveals the path of Yoga. O Mother, Victorious over the Three Worlds, grant me the fruit of Samādhi! Klīṃ, salutations to the Śūdra.
Having purified [it] with "maḥ svāhā," [one recites]: "oṃ amṛte amṛtopadbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtam ākarṣaya 2 siddhiṃ dehi amuka-padaṃ me vaśam ānaya svāhā."
Having purified it three times with the *itibhya* mantra, having joined the root [mantra] seven times above that,
having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, having displayed the *dhenu-yoni-mudrā*,
and having performed the directional protection (*digbandha*), [one should perform] the three *tālas* with finger-snaps (*koṭikā*).

Having warded off all obstacles with the blows of the heels of his divine vision moving before him, he satiated the venerable Guru in his own place and the venerable Goddess in his heart, [reciting]: *Oṃ vadavada vāgvādini mama jīvam*.
One should offer oblations into the mouth with this mantra: *Hvāgre sthirībhava sarvajanasattvavaśaṅkari svāhā*.
Then, having become filled with bliss (*ānandamaya*), adorned with red garments and other ornaments, one should [proceed] to the head...

Meditating on "I am Voham," having established the Śrīcakra in front of oneself, and having covered it with a handful of flowers while reciting the root mantra, one should offer a bali-oblation to the spirits in front of one's left side, saying: "O spirits who dwell here upon this earth..."

Having taken the *liṅga* and employed it according to the rules, one should arrange for residence elsewhere and say, "May they forgive me; salutations to them," thus dismissing the spirits (*bhūtas*). Then, [placing] perfumes, flowers, and so forth on one's right side...

Having sprinkled fragrant water and the articles of worship on the left with "Hāṃ Huṃ Phaṭ," and having looked [at them] with the divine gaze while recollecting the *nārāca-mudrā*, one should [hold] the water-pitcher with the left hand, saying "Āṃ."
Having touched the water situated there with the tip of the right hand,
saying "Raṃ," and having touched the flame of the lamp, saying "Raṃ," and having washed both hands,
[one should place] "Oṃ gurubhyo namaḥ" on the left and "Gaṃ gaṇa... on the right.

Having prostrated with "Salutation to the one who causes [the deity] to fall" in the center and "Salutation to the venerable family deity (Śrī-kuladevatā)," and having performed the *saṃghaṭṭa-mudrā* at the crown of the head,
one should worship the venerable Guru upon the head with the Śrī-guru-mantra and with perfumes and other offerings.

Having displayed the mudrās for the incense and other offerings, one performs the salutation with: *oṃ namo'stu gurave tasmai iṣṭadevasvarūpiṇe | yasya vāg-amṛtaṃ haṃti viṣaṃ saṃsārasaṃjñakam*. Thus ends the salutation.

Having prostrated to the deities and struck the ground three times with the left heel, one should perform the binding of the ten directions (*daśadigbandhana*) by first clapping three times above the head with the middle and index fingers, and then making the sound of the index finger and thumb;
having thus dispelled all obstacles with divine vision, [one should visualize] the form of a trident.

Having performed three circumambulations around one's own head with the two hands joined at the rays [of light], one should create the three fire-walls of the four classes of monks and perform three *prāṇāyāmas*. Therein, having fixed the mind on the *mūlādhāra* and holding the right nostril with the right thumb, one should recite the *praṇava* or the root mantra sixteen times.
Having filled the air through the left nostril and held the left nostril with the two little fingers,
one should retain the air through both openings while reciting that same mantra sixty-four times.
Having exhaled [the breath] again (once more for sixty-four times),

and having again held that same [breath] for half [that duration], while reciting "Oṃ Caṃ Paṃ Pṛ" thirty times, one should block the left nostril and inhale the air through the right nostril; this is one *prāṇāyāma*.
The second [breath] is performed in the reverse order of the first;
thus, having contemplated one's own body as entirely free from all impurities through these three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), one performs the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).

One should meditate thus, visualizing oneself as worthy of propitiating one's chosen deity, and then perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths). *Oṃ*, for this *Śrī Prāṇapratiṣṭhā Mantra*, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are the seers (*ṛṣayaḥ*).

Having performed the *añjali* (joining of palms) with the following: "The *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas are the meters; the Supreme Prāṇa-Śakti is the deity; *Āṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *Hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*); *Krauṃ* is the peg (*kīlaka*); and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*)."
Having recollected [the mantra], one should place it: "Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the Sages" on the head; "to the meters Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman" on the face;
"to the deity Parā Prāṇaśakti, Oṃ, salutation" on the heart. (pṛ. 20b) Oṃ.
*Vīja-yanamaḥ* to the secret place; *hrīṃ śaktaye namaḥ* to the feet;
*krauṃ kīlakāya namaḥ* to the navel. This is the ritual application (*viniyoga*) for the purpose of the consecration of my vital breaths (*prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā*) in all limbs. Then: *Oṃ āṃ*.

*Hrīṃ krauṃ aṃ kaṃ 4ṃ*, salutation to the heart (*āṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*), which is the essence of ether, air, fire, water, and earth. *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ iṃ caṃ 4ṃ*, salutation to the head (*īṃ śirase*), which is the essence of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
*Rasesvāhā* 4ṃ *uṃ ṭaṃ* 4ṃ; to the self of hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell, *ūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* 4ṃ; *aiṃ taṃ* 4ṃ;
to the self of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals, *oṃ kavacāya huṃ* 4ṃ.
Oṃ paṃ 4ṃ, to the self of speech, grasping, excretion, locomotion, and bliss, auṃ, to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ 4ṃ; aṃ yaṃ 9,
to the self of mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness, aḥ, to the weapon, phaṭ.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of these mantras from the thumbs to the palms of both hands—namely *oṃ caṃ paṃ* [and so on]—one should likewise place these same mantras upon the six limbs, beginning with the heart (*hṛdaya*).

Then, from the navel down to the two feet, [one places] *āṃ namaḥ* four times, and at the heart...
