Beginning with *dā* and ending with *nābhi*, from the crown of the head down to the heart: *krauṃ namaḥ*.
In the center of the heart-lotus: *yaṃ tvagātmane namaḥ*. On the eastern petal: *raṃ asṛgātmane namaḥ*. On the western petal: [raṃ asṛgātmane namaḥ].
Oṃ *laṃ* to the self consisting of flesh, salutation to Agni; *vaṃ* to the self consisting of fat, salutation to Vāyu; *śaṃ* to the self consisting of bone, salutation to Īśāna;
*ṣaṃ* to the self consisting of marrow, salutation to Nairṛta; *saṃ* to the self consisting of semen, salutation to [Varuṇa].

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) thus: "Haṃ, obeisance to the self of prāṇa" in the north; "Laṃ, obeisance to the self of jīva" in the south; and again in the pericarp, "Kṣaṃ, obeisance to the supreme self" (*paramātman*); one should meditate upon her as follows: *Oṃ ra...*

"I bow to the Goddess who is red in color, three-eyed, seated upon a lotus as red as the dawn and supported by four oceans, holding in her lotus-like hands a noose, a goad, a sword, an arrow, a trident, and a skull-cup."
Having meditated and placed the hand upon the heart, [one recites]: *oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ haṃsaḥ mama prāṇā iha prāṇāḥ 6 mama jīva iha sthitaḥ 6 mama sarvendriyāṇi iha sthitāni 6 ma*.

Having recited the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra— *oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ mama vāṅmanaḥ-tvak-cakṣuḥ-śrotra-ghrāṇa-prāṇā ihaivāgatya sukhaṃ ciraṃ tiṣṭhantu svāhā*— either three times or once, [one should contemplate] one's own body as light.
One should meditate on the *tiryag* [lineage]; this is the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).
Then, having performed the purification of body, speech, and mind with the mantra *oṃ āṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one should perform self-protection with *oṃ rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Then, having performed the recollection of one's own *mūla-mantra* and so forth, one should perform the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*. In that regard, first, inhalation (*pūraka*) is performed with the vowels;
retention (*kuṃbhaka*) with the consonants from *ka* to *ma*; and exhalation (*recaka*) with the consonants from *ya* onwards. Thus it is said.
Having performed the *mātṛkā-prāṇāyāma*, [one should recite]: "Oṃ, of this venerable internal *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, Brahmā is the *ṛṣi*, the *gāyatrī* is the meter,
the venerable *Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī* is the deity, and the consonants are the seed-syllables (*vīja*)."

The Suras are the Śaktis; the Unmanifest (Avyakta) is the Kīlaka. "I perform the Nyāsa as a limb of my worship of Śrī Cāmuṇḍā"—having thus spoken with palms joined in reverence and having meditated, one should perform the Nyāsa: "Obeisance to Brahmā, the Seer (Ṛṣi)," on the head; "Obeisance to Gāyatrī," on the mouth... [and so forth].

To the deity Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī, who is the essence of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas (*yattrīchandasena*), *namaḥ* at the face; to the seed-syllables which are the consonants (*halbhyaḥ vījebhyaḥ*), *namaḥ* at the heart;
to the powers which are the vowels (*svarāḥ śaktibhyaḥ*), *namaḥ* at the feet; to the unmanifest (*avyakta*) as the *kīlaka*, [namaskāra] at the private parts.

Salutation at the navel; this is the application for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as the limbs of Śrī Cāmuṇḍā upon all parts of the body. Now, the six-limbed ritual for the hands: *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ kaṃ 5 āṃ*—salutation (*namaḥ*) with the two thumbs; *4ṃ iṃ caṃ īṃ*—*svāhā* with the two index fingers.

4ṃ uṃ ṭaṃ 5ṃ ūṃ [to] the two middle fingers vaṣaṭ; 4ṃ aiṃ taṃ 5 aiṃ [to] the two ring fingers hum; oṃ paṃ 5 auṃ [to] the two little fingers vauṣaṭ; 4ṃ aṃ yaṃ 9ṃ aḥ [to] the palms and backs of the hands.

...bhyāṃ phaṭ. In this manner, one should also perform the placement (nyāsa) on the heart and other parts. Then: *Oṃ*, [visualize] a lotus whose pericarp consists of the letters of the sky, moon, and taste (five), which flashes with pairs of vowels as its filaments, and within whose petals are the five groups of consonants (*ka* to *ma*, *ca* to *ña*, *ṭa* to *ṇa*, *ta* to *na*, and *pa* to *ma*), along with the three [groups] beginning with *ya*, *śa*, and *ṣa*.
From the sequence of the *ṛ* sound,

[arises] the lotus of the letter *va*, situated upon the head, surrounded by the city of the earth (*jvākṣoṇīpura*), with its stalk and petals well-formed in the directions; it destroys poison and disease and conquers death, [located] on the path of the *mūlādhāra*.
Having heard this, one should meditate upon the awakened Śaśikuṇḍalī,
who is of the nature of subtle, blazing light resembling a fire, appearing like lightning, and touching the crown-lotus from the *mūlādhāra*; by her [touch],...

From the lotus of his six faces, the syllables of the Mātṛkā, whose nature is nectar, emerge in the form of *oṃ caṃ paṃ pṛ*. Having meditated upon them as pervading the body through the path of the Suṣumṇā,
and having thus visualized them all, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

Having meditated upon that subtle form consisting of the three [syllables], one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) with *aṃ namaḥ* and so forth. On the sixteen-petaled [lotus] at the throat: *kaṃ namaḥ*, *caṃ namaḥ*, *ṭaṃ namaḥ*, *ṭhaṃ namaḥ*. In the twelve-petaled [lotus] of the *anāhata*: *ḍaṃ namaḥ*, *ḍhaṃ*...

*Namaḥ* to *ṇaṃ*, *namaḥ* to *taṃ*, *namaḥ* to *paṃ*, *namaḥ* to *phaṃ*. On the ten petals of the navel: *namaḥ* to *baṃ*, *namaḥ* to *bhaṃ*, *namaḥ* to *maṃ*, *namaḥ* to *yaṃ*, *namaḥ* to *raṃ*, *namaḥ* to *laṃ*. At the root of the *liṅga* on the six petals: *namaḥ* to *vaṃ*, *namaḥ* to *śaṃ*.

*Namaḥ ṣaṃ namaḥ saṃ namaḥ* at the four-petalled *mūlādhāra*; *haṃ namaḥ kṣaṃ namaḥ* at the two-petalled [cakra] between the eyebrows—this concludes the placement (*nyāsa*) of the internal *mātṛkās*. Now follows the external *mātṛkā-nyāsa*. Regarding that:
The meditation on the syllable *Oṃ* and so forth is as before. As it is said:
"To her whose face, arms, feet, heart, belly, chest, and forehead are fashioned from the fifty distinct letters;
who possesses radiant matted hair and is adorned with a digit of the moon."

I bow to Bhāratī, who is as radiant as a refined fire, whose excellent hands hold a rosary, a sacrificial ladle, a water-pot, and a book, whose eyes are like lotuses, who dwells upon a lotus, who is pure as the *amṛtakalpa* tree, and who bears the weight of full breasts and hips.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the nyāsa: *hsauḥ ām* and so on, ending with *kṣam*;
*hsauḥ ām* and so on, ending with *kṣam*; and *hsauḥ*, placing these from the east onwards in their respective directions. Then: *4ṃ aṃ namaḥ* on the head. *4ṃ*.

Āṃ namaḥ to the face; 4ṃ iṃ namaḥ to the right eye; 4ṃ īṃ namaḥ to the left [eye]; 4ṃ uṃ 2 to the right ear; 4ṃ ūṃ 2 to the left ear; 4ṃ ṛṃ 2 to the right nostril; 4ṃ ṝṃ 2 to the left [nostril]; 4ṃ ḷṃ...
On the right cheek: 4ṃ Ḷṃ 2; on the left: 4ṃ Eṃ 2; on the upper lip: 4ṃ Aiṃ 2;
on the lower lip: 4ṃ Oṃ 2; on the upper teeth: 4ṃ Auṃ 2; on the lower teeth: 4ṃ Aṃ 2; on the forehead: 4ṃ Aḥ 2; on the tongue: 4ṃ Kaṃ 2.

Oṃ caṃ paṃ at the root of the right arm; 4ṃ khaṃ 2 at the elbow; 4ṃ gaṃ 2 at the wrist; 4ṃ jhaṃ 2 at the base of the fingers; 4ṃ ñaṃ 2 at the tips of the fingers; 4ṃ ṭaṃ 2 at the groin of the right leg; 4ṃ ṭhaṃ 2 at the knee; 4ṃ ḍaṃ 2.

*Ulphe* 4ṃ *ḍhaṃ* *namaḥ* at the base of the fingers; 4ṃ *ṇaṃ* 2 at the tips of the fingers; 4ṃ *paṃ* 2 on the sides of the wings; 4ṃ *phaṃ* 2 on the left; 4ṃ *vaṃ* 2 on the back; 4ṃ *bhaṃ* 2 at the navel; 4ṃ *maṃ* 2 in the belly; 4ṃ *yaṃ* [at] the limbs.
4ṃ Raṃ, obeisance to the self consisting of blood in the right shoulder;

4ṃ Laṃ, obeisance to the self consisting of flesh at the back of the neck; 4ṃ Vaṃ, obeisance to the self consisting of fat in the left shoulder; 4ṃ Śaṃ, obeisance to the self consisting of bone [in the heart].
*Namaḥ* from the heart to the right hand: *4ṃ ṣaṃ majjātmane namaḥ*.
*Namaḥ* from the heart to the left hand: *4ṃ saṃ śukrātmane namaḥ*. *Namaḥ* from the heart to the right foot: *4ṃ haṃ prāṇātmane*.
*Namaḥ* from the heart to the left foot: *4ṃ laṃ jīvātmane namaḥ*.
(24b) *Namaḥ* from the feet to the navel: *4ṃ kṣaṃ paramātmane namaḥ*. *Namaḥ* from the navel to the front [of the head]: thus is the *śuddhamātṛkā-nyāsa*.
He should perform other nyāsas according to his ability;
then follows the yoga-pīṭha-nyāsa. Therein, the yoga-pīṭha consists of four legs fashioned from the two *āsanas* and the two *rudras*, [placed] upon one's own body.

Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*): at the *mūlādhāra*, "4ṃ namaḥ maṇḍūkāya" (Oṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ, salutation to Maṇḍūka); at the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, "4ṃ namaḥ kālāgnirudrāya" (Oṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ, salutation to Kālāgnirudra);
at the *maṇipūra*, "4ṃ namaḥ mūlaprakṛtyai" (Oṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ, salutation to Mūlaprakṛti); at the *anāhata*... [the text continues].
*Oṃ dhāraśaktaye namaḥ* at the heart; *oṃ kūrmāya namaḥ* in that same place; *oṃ anantāya namaḥ*; *oṃ varāhāya namaḥ*;
*oṃ pṛthivyai namaḥ*. Therein, starting from the west and proceeding in reverse order: *oṃ...*
Salutation to the ocean of sugarcane juice; salutation to the ocean of wine;
salutation to the ocean of clarified butter; salutation to the ocean of milk.
In the center of that, [the syllable] *āṃ* and so forth, nine times.
Salutation to the island consisting of the nine jewels, adorned with gold;
to its west, [salutation] to the flower-jewel: aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ; 4ṃ ḷṃ uṃ, salutation to the lapis lazuli jewel; to the south, 4ṃ kaṃ 4ṃ.
Salutation to the sapphire gem in the southeast; 4ṃ Caṃ 4ṃ, salutation to the coral gem in the east;
4ṃ Ṭaṃ 5, salutation to the pearl gem in the northeast; 4ṃ Taṃ 5, salutation to the emerald gem in the north. 4ṃ...
Paṃ 5 Vajraratnāya namaḥ 2 in the northwest (vāyavye).
4ṃ Yaṃ 4 Go made ratnāya 2. In the central section (madhyakhaṇḍe): 4ṃ Śaṃ 4 Padmarāgaratnāya namaḥ 2. In that same central section: 4ṃ Suvarṇaparvatā.

Ya 2, for the Nandana garden; 2, in its center, 4ṃ, for the Kalpavṛkṣa trees; 2, in their center, 4ṃ, for the six seasons beginning with spring; 2, to its west, 4ṃ, for the horses of the senses; 2, to its east...
pṛ0 25ba) To all the elephants of the sense-objects, *oṃ* 4ṃ *namaḥ*. In their midst:
*oṃ* 4ṃ *namaḥ* to the ground of variegated jewels (2); *oṃ* 4ṃ *namaḥ* to the surrounding moat of the water of compassion; *oṃ* 4ṃ *namaḥ* to the golden rampart (2); *oṃ* 4ṃ *ci*...
To the Cintāmaṇi-gṛha (the wish-fulfilling jewel palace), twice; to the cremation ground, twice;
to the Pārijāta tree, twice; in its center, to the jeweled altar (ratnavedikā), twice;
upon that, to the jeweled pedestal (maṇipīṭha), twice; in the four directions, to the Nāga... [twice].
Salutations to the hosts of sages. Salutations to the various gods.
Salutations to those who delight in much flesh, bones, and so forth. Salutations to the corpses, skulls, funeral pyres, and bones.

Above that, having placed the heart mantra "Oṃ śvetacchatrāya svāhā" twice and "Oṃ ratnasiṃhāsanāya svāhā" twice, [one places them] on the right shoulder "Oṃ dharmāya svāhā" twice, on the left shoulder "Oṃ jñānāya svāhā" twice, and on the left thigh "Oṃ... twice.
For detachment (vairāgya), twice on the right thigh; for sovereignty (aiśvarya), twice on the face;
for non-dharma (adharma), twice on the left side; for ignorance (ajñāna), twice on the navel;
for non-detachment (avairāgya), twice on the right side; for non-sovereignty (anaiśvarya), [twice].

Furthermore, in the heart: *yaṃ* 2, to Māyā 2, to Vidyā 2, *haṃ* 4, to Ananta 2, to Dharma 2, *haṃ* 4, to Ānandakanda 2, *haṃ* 4, to Saṃvinnāla 2, *haṃ* 4, salutation to the petals consisting of Prakṛti. *Haṃ* 4.

Salutation to the filaments consisting of transformations (vikṛtimaya-kesara). 2. 4ṃ. Salutation to the pericarp (karṇikā) formed of the fifty letters. Aṃ. Salutation to the solar disc (arka-maṇḍala).
Saṃ. Salutation to the lunar disc (soma-maṇḍala). Raṃ. Salutation to the fiery disc (vahni-maṇḍala).
Salutation to the collective being; salutation to passion (*rajas*); salutation to darkness (*tamas*);
salutation to the self (*ātman*); salutation to the inner self (*antarātman*); salutation to the supreme self (*paramātman*); salutation to the self of knowledge (*jñānātman*); salutation to *māyā*.
*Tattvāya namaḥ*, *Kaṅkālātattvāya namaḥ*, *Vidhyātattvāya namaḥ*, *Paratattvāya namaḥ*. Then, one should worship the nine *pīṭha-śaktis* in the eight directions and in the center, as follows: [2ṃ].
Salutation to Jayā; salutation to Vijayā; salutation to Ajitā;
salutation to Aparājitā; salutation to Nityā; salutation to Vilāsinī; salutation to Dogdhī; salutation to Aghorā—thus [is the worship].

Then, having worshipped in the eight directions starting from the east, one performs the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) in the center with the mantras: "Obeisance to Maṅgalā" and "Obeisance to the Lotus-Seated One, the Embodiment of All Powers.
Regarding the determination of the directions therein, the "east" is defined as the direction facing the worshipper and the object of worship.

According to the scriptural injunctions, one should contemplate oneself and others as facing east; likewise, in the worship of the goddess Adharmādipūjanī and in the adoration of the [divine] forms, one faces east.
Now follows the determination regarding the pedestal: the daily worship is performed upon a śālagrāma stone, a gem, or a yantra.
One should perform the worship according to the prescribed rite upon a golden image or any other image duly installed, ranging in size from the thumb up to a span (vitasti),
within a shrine for images that is neither burnt nor cracked, and which is not tilted upward or downward.
"Oṃ caṃ0 paṃ pṛ0 27a) One should perform the invocation (āvāhana) there at the Liṅga, which is smooth and devoid of a base. Herein lies the specific rule for the Pañcāyatana system:
"In the case of the Pañcāyatana system, one should worship Viṣṇu in the center thereafter."

In the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast, one should place Gaṇanāyaka, Ravi, Śivā, and Śiva; in the center, Gaṇeśa, Śiva, Śivā, Ravi, and Viṣṇu; and in the middle [of that], Vighna, Jana, and Gaṇeśvara.
When Bhavānī is situated in the center, one should first worship Īśa, Vighna, Arka, and Mādhava;
when the Sun is situated in the center, one should worship Gaṇeśa, Girijā, and Acyuta;
and from that [sequence], one should worship Gaṇeśa and the others located in the center.
Saying "Jaya," one should perform the ritual services such as invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth;
then, having taken a handful of flowers and meditated upon the Goddess in one's own heart, she reaches the *brahmarandhra* by way of the *suṣumṇā*. Then, from there...

Having joined the Goddess, who has emerged through the *sāraṃdhra*, with the handful of flowers and the Mātṛkās, one should then recite the root mantra: "O Supreme Goddess, I invoke you, the unborn and pure one, established within myself, as the sacrificial fire, manifest in bodily form."

Reciting, "O Goddess of gods, who are easily attained through devotion, who are intent upon the supreme rasa, remain very firm for as long as I shall worship you," he should offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) upon the pedestal.

The invocation (*āvāhana*) therein is the specific detail; in the case of the *sāligrāma* or a stationary [liṅga], there is no invocation or dismissal (*visarjana*). Then, having praised the majesty of that form with the root mantra, one should cultivate devotion toward all the limbs of Śivā.
"Drawn forth by affection, I establish you as a lamp"— with these words,
one should establish [the deity] with the *sthāpinī-mudrā*. "O Goddess, the inner controller of all, auspicious and consisting of all seeds, I [establish] you within myself..."
"I prepare this supremely pure seat. [Recite] the root mantra. "O Goddess, seated comfortably upon this excellent seat, you whose nature is the Imperishable (Akṣara);
O Sovereign of Devas, remain here; O Supreme Goddess, be gracious, O Blessed One. [Oṃ caṃ paṃ pṛ. 28a) [Remain here, O Sovereign of Devas; be gracious, O Supreme Goddess, O Blessed One.]
Then, having performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) upon the limbs of the Goddess, one should perform the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*).
Reciting the root mantra, one should perform the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) with the *dhenumudrā*. Then, [one should perform it] with the *lelihānamudrā*.

One should perform the *jjīvananyāsa* as follows: *Āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ oṃ kṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ hrīṃ oṃ haṃsaḥ*. Oṃ *hrīṃ krauṃ*, [17] *caṇḍikāyāḥ prāṇā iha prāṇāḥ*. Oṃ *hrīṃ krauṃ*, *caṇḍikāyāḥ jīva iha*.
Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ 17; may all the sense organs of Caṇḍikā remain steady.
Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ 17; may the speech, mind, eyes, ears, tongue, nose, and vital breaths of Caṇḍikā remain here for a long time, free from movement and in a state of bliss.

Having performed the *jīvan-nyāsa* with "Svāhā," and then having displayed the *khaḍga*, *muṇḍa*, *abhaya*, *śaṅkha*, *dhenu*, and *yoni* mudrās, one should perform the services (*upacāra*) beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*).
[Recite] the root mantra: "O supreme bliss, which arises from contact with the line of devotion!"

O Source of all existence, I offer this water for the feet (*pādya*) to the dust of Your lotus-like feet; O Blessed One, may it purify You. To the source of the Vedas, the teacher of the Vedas, the divine self of the gods—to You, I offer this water for sipping (*ācamana*). *Pṛ0 28ba)* *saṃbhavaḥ tasmaite caraṇābjāyapādyaṃ śuddhāyaka lpaye bhagavate etatte pādyaṃ namaḥ | mūlaṃ vedānāmapi vedāya devānāṃ devatātmane ācamam ||*

I prepare water for sipping (ācamanīya) with the mantra *svadhā* for the sake of the purity of those who are already pure; I prepare the ninefold water offering (arghya), which is divine, characterized by supreme bliss, free from the three-fold suffering,
and the root that removes the three-fold suffering.

O Blessed One, may this arghya be for you, svāhā! O Root, for the one who is free from all impurity, for my own self which is perfectly complete—O God, I prepare this madhuparka; be gracious to me, O nectar-like madhuparka!

Even for one who is defiled by remnants or impure, through the mere remembrance of him [the Lord], one attains purity; for him, this is the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka). O Blessed One, here is the water for sipping, which is nectar. Now, another... [pari]
After the sipping of water (*ācamana*), the bathing, the garment, and the sacred thread (*upavīta*), he says:

"Oṃ caṃ paṃ... (pṛ. 29a). After the food offering (*naivedya*), he mentions the substances to be deposited for the foot-water (*pādya*) and so forth, saying: "Śyāmāka, viṣṇukrāntā, lotus, and dūrvā grass are for the *pādya*."
One should place cloves, nutmeg, and *kaṅkola* in the water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamanīya*).

In the vessel for the *arghya* offering, one should place *urvā* grass, sesame seeds, the tips of *darbha* grass, barley, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*). And in the vessel for the *madhuparka*, [one should place honey, curd, and ghee].
One should add curd, ghee, and honey; however, in the absence of the substances for the *pādya* and other offerings, one should likewise sprinkle them with water.
This is the determination of the substances for the feet and so forth.
Then, having lifted the Goddess [from the pedestal] with fragrant oil and turmeric, [one should perform the ritual] with the root mantra...
O Mother, O Bhagavatī, whose very form is the fragrance of supreme bliss, I offer this bath along with all its limbs and sub-limbs;
reciting the root mantra, one should pour water from the conch in equal portions.
One should consecrate the Goddess ten times with water. Then, [the mantra for] the *ācamana* is:
*Mūlam Māyā Citrapaṭacchinnanijaguhyatatejase*. [The mantra for] the upper garment (*uttarīya*) is: "O Nirāvaraṇavāma, I offer this upper garment to You. *Bha*... [p. 29b]
Having thus offered the garment, the rule for the rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) regarding garments is as follows:
yellow for Viṣṇu, white for Śambhu, and red for Vighna, Arka, and Śakti; one should discard a garment that is torn, soiled, or worn out, as well as one treated with oil and the like.
That whose root is thus corrupted, by whose three powers this entire universe is woven together— let these [acts] constitute the sacrificial thread for him who has the sacrificial thread as his body;
let there be the sacrificial thread, the upper garment, and the ritual sipping of water.

O Goddess worshipped by the immortals, whose nature is the substratum of the power of various forms of beautiful passion, whose essence is the root of all things, I fashion for You, O Blessed One, diverse ornaments and equalized decorations.

One should place those letters from *a* to *kṣa*, encapsulated by the root mantra (*mūla*), upon the limbs of the deity; this yoga is the "delusion" (*mohana*) in the world. The root mantra is [the essence] completely filled with the fragrance of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).
Oṃ Caṃ Paṃ Pṛ (30a): "O Supreme Goddess, O Blessed One, out of compassion, please accept this stainless fragrance. Having thus offered the fragrance with the little finger and the thumb, then—
One should display the fragrance mudrā. O Supreme Goddess, accept this unbroken rice, saffron, and nutmeg offered by me through my grace; O Bhagavatī, [accept] the unbroken... the root mantra.
One should display this mudrā with the index, middle, and thumb fingers,
saying: "Let this root, born from the forest of trees, possessing manifold qualities and captivating the mind, this flower of blissful fragrance, be accepted."

Having offered these flowers to the Blessed One, one should display the flower-mudrā using the index finger and thumb; if capable, the wise person should offer dūrvā grass, arka, or mandāra flowers up to the knee. [One should offer] flowers, leaves, or fruit.
One should not offer the *laṃ* deity with a downward-facing flower, nor [offer] water;
thus, having likewise satiated that [deity] who has been so worshipped, one should perform the worship with flowers three times and then make the offering.
According to the statement "the worship of the enclosure," one should worship Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, or Mahāsarasvatī at the central seed-syllable (bīja),
and having worshipped [them] at the right-hand seed-syllables, [one recites] the root-mantra (mūla) as consciousness (saṃvit).
"O Goddess, O you who are fond of the supreme nectar-essence, grant me permission for this worship of the retinue. Having thus requested permission,
[one should worship] with scents and unbroken rice grains (akṣata) at the heart, and with "agnau śirase svāhā" at the head.

Hā! Homage to the Goddess of the Head (Śirodevī) in the southwest (Nairṛta). Oṃ hrīṃ! Vaṣaṭ to the Crest (Śikhā) in the northwest (Vāyavya). Huṃ to the Armor (Kavaca) and to the Goddess of the Armor (Kavacadevī) in the northeast (Īśāna).
Vauṣaṭ to the Three Eyes (Netratraya) and to the Goddess of the Eyes (Netradevī).

*Purataḥ* (in front): *2ṃ astrāya phaṭ*, [offering] to the Weapon-deity (*astradevī*) in the cardinal directions. Thus is the worship of the limbs (*aṅgapūjana*). This is the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*). To the deities:
*Oṃ caṃ paṃ pṛbhyaḥ*, for the sake of all ritual offerings (*sarvopacāra*), [I offer] perfumes and unbroken rice grains (*gaṃdha-kṣatāni*). Samarpya.
Having prayed thus: "May these deities of the first enclosure,
together with their limbs, their retinues, and their weapons, being worshipped with all ritual offerings and satisfied, become the granters of boons," [one should then state] one's desired object.

"O Caṇḍikā, worshipped by the gods, may this [flower] offered with devotion, honored in the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*), be presented to you. Thus one should offer flowers to the Goddesses; this concludes the first enclosure. Therein, the Guru...

One should worship three rows or four gurus. As it has been stated: "Furthermore, in all the tantras, the gurus previously indicated are said to be those [to be worshipped] in the morning"; thus, as before, one should offer flowers and consecrated rice (akṣata).
One should perform the offering of a handful of flowers along with a prayer; this is the second enclosure. In the eastern corner of the triangle:
2ṃ to Sarasvatī and Brahmā; in the southwest corner: 2ṃ to Viṣṇu.
On the northwest, to Lakṣmī and Śrī: 2ṃ; to Śiva and Pārvatī on the north:
2ṃ; to Siṃha on the right: 2ṃ; to Mahiṣa: 2ṃ. This is the third enclosure. For the sake of all offerings to the deities: gaṃ.

One should offer oblations as before, praying for one's desired goal, and present a handful of flowers; this is the third enclosure. Then, one should worship in the six corners, proceeding clockwise starting from the east, as follows:
2ṃ Naṃ Nandajāyai, 2ṃ Raṃ Raktidāyai, 2ṃ Śāṃ Śākambharyai,
2ṃ Duṃ Durgāyai, 2ṃ Bhīṃ Bhīmāyai, 2ṃ Bhrāṃ Bhrāmaryai;
all else is as before— this is the fourth enclosure (caturthāvaraṇa).
Then, on the eight petals: 2ṃ vrāṃ to Brahmāṇī; 2ṃ māṃ to Māheśvarī; oṃ kauṃ to Kaumārī; 2ṃ vai to Vaiṣṇavī; 2ṃ vāṃ to Vārāhī;
2ṃ nāṃ to Nārasiṃhī; 2ṃ aiṃ to Raudrī; 2ṃ cāṃ to Cāmuṇḍā.
*Yai 2ṃ*, as before; thus ends the fifth enclosure.
*Oṃ caṃ paṃ* (pṛ0 32a). Then, on the twenty-four petals, proceeding clockwise starting from the east:
*2ṃ* to Viṣṇumāyā, *2ṃ* to Cetanā, *2ṃ* to Buddhi, *2ṃ* to Ni... [and so forth].

To Nidrā (Sleep) svāhā; to Kṣudhā (Hunger) svāhā; to Chāyā (Shadow) svāhā; to Śakti (Power) svāhā; to Tṛṣṇā (Thirst) svāhā; to Kṣānti (Patience) svāhā; to Jāti (Birth) svāhā; to Lajjā (Modesty) svāhā; to Śānti (Peace) svāhā; to Śraddhā (Faith) svāhā;
to Kānti (Beauty) svāhā; to Lakṣmī (Fortune) svāhā; to Dhṛti (Fortitude) svāhā; to Vṛtti (Conduct) svāhā; to Śruti (Sacred Tradition) svāhā.
To Tyai 2ṃ, Smṛtyai 2ṃ, Dayāyai 2ṃ, Tuṣṭyai 2ṃ, Puṣṭyai 2ṃ, and Mātre; the rest is as before. This is the sixth enclosure (ṣaṣṭāvaraṇa).
Then, in the corners of the Earth-mansion (bhūgṛha), starting from the southeast (āgneya) corner: 2ṃ Gaṅgā.
Ṇaṃ ṇaṃ to Gaṇapataye; 2ṃ kṣaṃ to Kṣetrapālāya; 2ṃ vaṃ to Vaṭukāya;
2ṃ yaṃ to Yoginībhyaḥ—all else as before.
This is the seventh enclosure (saptamāvaraṇam). Then, in the Bhūpura, starting from the east, in the eight directions...
KṢU 2Ṃ LAṂ to Indra; 2Ṃ RAṂ to Vahni; 2Ṃ ṬAṂ to Yamuna; 2Ṃ KṢAṂ to Nairṛti; 2Ṃ VAṂ to Varuṇa; 2Ṃ YAṂ to Vāyu; 2Ṃ SAṂ to Soma;
2Ṃ HAṂ to Īśāna; and 2Ṃ AṂ to Ananta.
Between Nairṛti and Paścima: 2ṃ Hrīṃ to Brahmā; between Pūrva and Īśāna: [2ṃ Hrīṃ to Brahmā]. Thus is the eighth enclosure (aṣṭamāvaraṇa).
8. 2ṃ Kaṃ to Vajra; 2ṃ Śaṃ to Śakti; 2ṃ Naṃ to Daṇḍa; 2ṃ Khaṃ.
Khaḍgarāya 2ṃ, Paṃpāśāya 2ṃ, AṃAṅkuśāya 2ṃ, GaṃGadāyai 2ṃ, TriṃTriśūlāya 2ṃ— thus in the eight directions.
CaṃCakrāya in the middle of the southwest and west, 2ṃ, PaṃPa...

*Āmāya* twice, between the East and the North; all else is as before. Thus ends the ninth enclosure (navamāvaraṇa). Then, having fully satiated the Goddess, one should perform the services beginning with incense (*dhūpa*) up to the final offering (*ucchaṣṭha*). As follows:
Having placed incense into the incense vessel and sprinkled the vessel with water using the *astra-mantra*, one should offer it with the word "Namaḥ. Then,
touching the incense vessel with the left index finger and taking the *arghya* water with the right hand...
Oṃ Caṃ Paṃ Pṛ. Having taken the root, this incense produced from the essence of the forest tree— rich in fragrance, most enchanting, and worthy of being smelled by all the gods—
may it be accepted, O Śrī Caṇḍī, together with your limbs and your retinue.

Having recited the mantra "kāyaidhūpaṃ samarpayāmi namaḥ," one should sprinkle water; while the right index finger and thumb are joined, one should display the incense mudrā (dhūpamudrā). Then [recite] the Jagaddhvani mantra.
Having worshipped the bell with the mantra "Mātaḥ svāhā," while ringing it with the left hand, one should proclaim the qualities of the deity; then,
with the right hand, one should offer incense at the navel of the deity.

Then one should offer water and a handful of flowers; thereafter, having lit a lamp, consecrated it with "phaṭ," and offered a flower with "namaḥ," the *arghya* is placed in the right hand by touching it with the middle finger of the left hand.
Taking water, [I offer] this great lamp, well-illuminated,
which removes the darkness of all [obstacles], a light that shines both externally and internally; may this lamp be accepted by [the Goddess], together with her limbs and her retinue.
Saying, "I offer a lamp to Śrī Caṇḍikā; obeisance," one should sprinkle water.
Having displayed the lamp-mudrā with the middle finger and thumb, everything else is as in the case of incense. Now, regarding the specific [details] concerning the lamp:

He said: "The ground for those who follow the right-hand path (dakṣiṇācāra) is even, whereas that of those who follow the left-hand path (vāmācāra) is uneven. A ghee lamp should be on the right, while an oil lamp is on the left;
because the wick is white on the right, it is red on the left."
Thus ends the lamp.

Then, having worshipped with the root mantra a maṇḍala consisting of a triangle and hexagon inscribed within a square in front of the deity, one should place there a vessel for the food offering (naivedya) made of gold or other materials, together with its base.

Having established the *raṃ* syllable there, one should serve milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and other foods mixed with clarified butter and sugar according to one's capacity; then, one should sprinkle it with water consecrated by the Astra-mantras. Next, one should cover it with the Cakra-mudrā, and then with the Astra...

One should sprinkle it with water consecrated by mantras; then, having visualized the seed-syllable of air (Yaṃ) in the right hand and reciting it seven times, one should dry up the defects of the food offering (*naivedya*); then, having visualized the seed-syllable of fire (Raṃ) in the right hand and touched it, [one should burn them away].
Having placed [the hand] upon the palm of the other, one burns away the defects of the food offering by reciting the twelve-syllable mantra (*arka-japa*).

Then, having meditated on the nectar-seed syllable (*amṛta-bīja*) in the left hand while reciting "vaṃ," which is the nectar-seed syllable, [one sprinkles it] with the stream of nectar arising from that.
Having rendered it inert (*mṛtīkṛtya*), one should then consecrate it eight times with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*),
display the *dhenumudrā*, and then worship the food offering (*naivedya*) with perfumes and flowers.
Then, having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the *Śrīcakra*, [one should worship] the Goddess...

Having reflected upon that which has arisen from that, and having touched the vessel of the *naivedya* with the left thumb, one should take the *arghya* water in the right hand and offer the root mantra along with the food prepared in that excellent vessel—
consisting of various and manifold delicacies.
"O Goddess of gods, together with your attendants, may you accept this food offering (naivedya), along with your limbs and your retinue, for the sake of the deity Śrī Caṇḍikā;
Svāhā! Having said this, one should offer water, and then [touch] the thumb...

Having displayed the *naivedya-mudrā* with the two *nāmikā* fingers, and then having touched the *naivedya* vessel with both hands joined by flowers, one should offer it with the mantra: "O Goddess of Gods, together with your retinue, I offer this; please accept it."
Reciting this mantra three times, one should lift up the vessel; then,
having offered a flower, one should display the *padmābhā* mudrā with the left hand,
and then display the *prāṇa* and other mudrās with the right hand.

One should offer oblations as follows: with the little finger, ring finger, and thumb, "Oṃ prāṇāya svāhā"; with the index finger, middle finger, and thumb, "Oṃ apānāya svāhā"; and with the ring finger [and thumb], "Oṃ udānāya svāhā."
With the middle finger and thumb: *oṃ vyānāya svāhā*; with the index finger: *oṃ caṃ* [etc. (as on folio 35a); with the middle, ring, and thumb: *oṃ samānāya svāhā*;
and with all five fingers—having thus displayed these mudrās, one should then [remove] the curtain.
Having held [the vessel] eight times with the root mantra, one should then recite the root mantra:
"O Sovereign of the gods of all gods, supreme cause of satisfaction for all, filled with unbroken bliss, accept this excellent water, together with your limbs and your retinue."
Having offered water with the mantra "To Śrī Caṇḍikā, svāhā," he should then gaze at the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) located in the southeast corner with the root mantra,
perform sprinkling and striking with "phaṭ," and touch it with kuśa grass while reciting "hum."
Then, having established the fire there by means of its root-mantra, having invoked the deity into that fire,
and having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, [he recites] *oṃ bhūḥ svāhā*, *oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā*, *oṃ svaḥ svāhā*, and *oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā*— thus the Vyāhṛtis.
Having offered four oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*, then having offered twenty-five oblations with the root mantra (*mūla*), and again having offered four oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*,
one should then enjoin the Goddess into the form (*mūrti*).

Having dismissed [the fire], one should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya); thereafter, one should perform the offering of the bali. Then, in the four corners of the Śrīyantra, starting from the southeast, one should draw triangles containing the Māyā-bīja and hexagons.

Having fashioned the mandalas and worshipped them with "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the pervasive mandala," one should then place the vessel for the bali offering upon the fire-mandala and worship it with "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the bali substance."
Then, having touched the offering with the left thumb and forefinger and meditating on it as being held in the hand, [one recites]: "Come, come, O Goddess’s son Vaṭukanātha,
radiant with a mass of tawny matted locks and possessing three eyes!"

Jvālāmukha, destroy all obstacles! Destroy! Accept this bali-offering accompanied by all ritual services! Svāhā! This bali is for Vaṭukanātha; obeisance! May he be satisfied by the offering of this bali.
"Oṃ caṃ paṃ, O Lord of the Triangle, may all accomplishments, peace, contentment, and nourishment be mine through your grace. Thus one should offer a handful of flowers.
This is the *vaṭuka-bali*. Then, one should place the *bali* offering upon the *nairṛta*-maṇḍala.

Having established the *raṃbali* and worshipped it with "Oṃ hrīṃ balidravyāya namaḥ," then, having touched the *bali* with the left thumb, middle finger, and ring finger, [one recites] "From above the Egg of Brahmā... and so forth, [addressing] whichever Yoginī [is intended].
*Oṃ namo sarvayoginībhyaḥ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
"This is the offering for the Yoginīs; homage! Thus is the offering to the Yoginīs.
Then, in the wind-maṇḍala: *raṃ*; in the pervasive maṇḍala: *raṃ*; *vyā*.

Having worshipped with "Obeisance to the abode of all auspiciousness," and having established the vessel for the *bali* offering there, one should worship with "Obeisance to the substance of the *bali* offering" (*oṃ balidravyāya namaḥ*),
and then touch the *bali* with the left thumb and ring finger.

Oṃ kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣaiṃ kṣauṃ kṣaḥ! O Kṣetrapāla, together with all your attendants, accept this bali, accept it! Svāhā! "This bali is for Kṣetrapāla; obeisance!"—thus ends the bali offering to Kṣetrapāla.

Then, having worshipped in the south-western mandala with "Oṃ hrīṃ, to the pervasive mandala," and having placed the sacrificial offering (bali) upon its base there, having worshipped it with "Oṃ hrīṃ,
to the bali substances," then follows the central sacrifice.
Touched with the mudrā: Oṃ gāṃ gīṃ gūṃ gaiṃ gauṃ gaḥ, to Gaṇapati, the bestower of boons, bring all people under your control;
accept the bali! Svāhā! This is the bali for Gaṇa.
[Offer] the *bali* to Gaṇeśa with "To the Lord" (*pataye iti*).

Then, having prepared a mandala to the left of the Goddess as before and worshipped it, place the *bali* together with its support and worship it with "Oṃ hrīṃ, to the *bali* substance" (*oṃ hrīṃ validravyāya iti*). Then...
Having touched the offering with the *sthitimudrā*, [recite]: *oṃ hrīṃ sarvavighnakṛdbhyaḥ sarvabhūtebhyaḥ svāhā*. "This offering is for all beings;
*oṃ caṃ paṃ* [etc.]... obeisance. This is the offering to all beings (*sarvabhūtabali*). Then, [offer] flowers to the goddesses.

Having offered this divine water, naturally pure, very cool, and contained within a golden vessel, which has been presented by me to you— O Śrī Caṇḍī, together with your limbs and retinue— please accept this excellent water.

Then, having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*), one should consider the food offering (*naivedya*) to have lost its essence and offer the remains (*ucchiṣṭa*) with the mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālyai namaḥ*.
After that, having washed both hands, [one should recite] the root mantra for her.
May this betel leaf, rippled with portions of lime,
camphor, and areca nut, and enriched with fragrant substances, be accepted as *tāmbūla* for Śrī Caṇḍikā, together with her limbs and her retinue; may it be mine.
There, having displayed the parasol, chowries, and other items, one should then perform the *nīrājana* ceremony.
Having prepared a triangular and eight-petaled mandala in a vessel made of gold or other materials, and having worshipped it with the root mantra, [one should worship] the eight petals.
(Page 37b) Having placed the single-footed [lamp] within the triangle from the lamp,
and having offered perfume, unbroken rice, flowers, fruit, betel, and so forth with the root mantra,
one then unifies the inner light and the outer light by means of the root mantra.
One should continuously perceive the lamp of the *Eva*-family through the sequence of the upper and lower [centers]. You are indeed the moon, the sun, the earth, lightning, and likewise fire;
thus, O Radiant One, you are the supreme light.
Reciting the mantra, "O Caṇḍikā,

let this offering be accepted for my success," one should ring the bell with the left hand and perform the *nīrājana* rite over the Goddess nine times, while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) ending in *svāhā*.
Having offered three handfuls of flowers with the mantra "To the glorious Caṇḍikā, together with her retinue,
[I offer] this handful of flowers," one should then recite the four verses with single-minded devotion.

That which is designated as growth along with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), like a mirror-surface, and that which is conceptualized by the various mental fluctuations (*manovṛtti*) in the form of satisfaction—such as sounds in the form of vocal music and so forth. (f. 38a) *Oṃ Caṃ Paṃ* *Pṛ*. 38a).
The students who cause division are fashioned from the lotus of his body;
the vital breaths (prāṇas) are the horses in the form of the Suṣumnā path for Śiva,
while the ego (ahaṃkāra) is the elephant, and the impulses (vegāḥ) are the reins.

The senses are the horses, with their respective forms such as sound and so forth; the mind is the reins; the intellect is the charioteer by virtue of its solar nature; and everything else is the chariot, which is thus equipped.
Having recited the verses beginning with "raṇātmanā," then having performed the *ṛṣi*, *chandas*, and *devatā* for the root mantra, as well as the heart-mantra and the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) ritual,
and having meditated as before, one should mutter the root mantra according to one's capacity.

Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) beginning with *tvaṃ pūrvavat* and having meditated [upon the deity], one should then take the water for the offering (*arghodaka*) in the right hand; reciting the mantra "guhyātiguhye" (p. 38b), one should offer it into the left hand of the Goddess. Then...
Having turned one's back toward the *argha* vessel and worshipped the conch with a flower, one should perform worship;
then, having prostrated before the Goddess like a staff (*daṇḍavat*), one should perform circumambulation. As it is said: "O Aja, Īśa, Śakti, and Gaṇapa..."
These [mantras] of the Bhāskaras, beginning with *vodāddhaṃca*, are for the purpose of the number of days and so forth for the sake of all success. Then one should recite the hymn;
one should recite the *Nityacaṇḍī-stava* spoken by Mārkaṇḍeya.
Reciting the *sthita-mūla-mantra*, one incurs no sin; furthermore,
with other hymns as well, one should offer special *argha* water,
holding it in the right hand, and then [offer it] after first [performing] *prāṇa-buddhi*.

Whatever has been thought by the mind, spoken by speech, performed by the hands, feet, belly, and genitals, while engaged in the duties of the body— whether in the states of waking, dreaming, or deep sleep— all that is remembered as having been done.
Oṃ caṃ paṃ (pṛ0 39a) brahmārpaṇaṃ bhavatu svāhā. Māṃ madīyaṃ sarvaṃ caṇḍikāyai te samarpaye. Oṃ tatsat.
Then, with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*: "Go, go to the supreme abode, to your own place..."
"O Rameśvarī, where even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, do not know that supreme state"— reciting this, one should lift up the Goddess in the form of light from the *nirmālya* flower,
smell it, and through the yoga of inhalation (*pūraka*), [place it] upon the thousand-petaled [lotus].
Having reached the lotus and meditated upon it, having brought [the deity] via the path of the *suṣumṇā* to the heart-lotus, [one should say]: "Stay,
stay in your own place, O Supreme Goddess, in that supreme abode where Brahmā and all others reside."
Having caused [the deity] to descend into one's heart and established him within the heart-lotus, one should recite the *Śāntistava*. Then,
having written the syllable *Hrīṃ* with water on the little toe below the seat, [one should place] the little toe...
"Whomever I touch with my hand,
whomever I behold with my eye— may he become a servant or a slave,
even if he were equal to Śakra," reciting this mantra, [apply] sesame seeds to the forehead.
"Having done what, may one dwell in happiness?"— thus, he who worships the Goddess three times a day while practicing the Dharma is never afflicted by hostile enemies,
being well-protected; such is the worship performed at the three times of day.

Those who are capable should perform this [worship] twice or even once; especially on festival days such as the *saṃkrānti*, one should worship the Goddess with ten or five types of offerings. One who is incapable should have it performed.

One who is capable of giving should offer the materials for worship; seeing another worshipping with equal devotion, one should have a mind fixed on that [worship]. Herein is written the sequence of the five-fold worship (pañcapūjā) spoken by Nārada, which serves as a means when resources are lacking.
The five states—Sīta, Urva, Sūtakī, Ārtā, and Ripā—are taught;
that worship is proclaimed in sequence. Regarding the means of worship (*pūjāsādhana*), [the mantra] "Oṃ Caṃ Paṃ" (p. 40a), by means of the pride of the self alone, that worship... [is performed].
One who is terrified by the absence of pure means of accomplishment should worship the Goddess with whatever offerings are available, or even mentally; for she,
when known through the *Sāvitrī*, bestows complete success upon both the young and the old.

Women and fools [are excluded] from that [knowledge] due to their lack of understanding; however, just as the wise perform the worship of the gods through knowledge, so too should a man who is in a state of birth-impurity (sūtakī) bathe and perform the mental *saṃdhyā*—
the mental [worship].

One who has desires should worship; one free from desire should perform everything. During the period of impurity (*sūtaka*), as stated by Sūta, one who is afflicted by diseases should neither bathe nor worship.
However, having beheld the form of the illustrious Goddess or the solar disc, even once, one should [perform the rite].
Having recited the mantra over the flower, one should cast it there;
then, having bathed and worshipped the Guru and the twice-born, one should pray to them: "May the fault of interrupting my worship not befall me."
Having received blessings from them, one should worship the Goddess Śī as before.
These five modes of worship, beginning with the Āsurī, have been proclaimed by Nārada.
He who, having personally prepared all the ritual implements, performs them with faith—

One who is devoted to worshipping the Goddess shall easily obtain all fruits; the fruit of worship arises from the act itself, whereas other means are merely for the sake of providing the materials. Therefore, having personally procured the requisites, one should perform the worship.
A man who is devoid of the worship of the Goddess shall fall into hell;
therefore, the worship of the Goddess must be performed with faith, in whatever manner possible.
Thus ends [the work] from the service of the lotus feet of the illustrious Rāmakokila.
The *Śrīmaccaṇḍikārcanapaddhati* composed by Keṇagovindarāma is hereby completed.
Śrī Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, Mother of the World, Caṇḍikā.

I shall now speak the armor (*kavaca*), which contains the essence of mantras, known as *Jayā*, which pervades the three worlds; it is supreme, secret, and not to be disclosed—by whom has it ever been told by me? Without this, there can be no accomplishment through the armor.
Namo Īśvarī! This must not be spoken and must not be given to the wicked or to a non-practitioner.
The Śrī Devī said: "O Lord of the Three Worlds, this has been told by me in many ways; this grace has been bestowed by you yourself."
O Lord Śrī Bhairava, we have performed our prostrations;
at dawn, at midday, in the evening, and at midnight, this supreme armor (*kavaca*) containing the mantra should be recited, along with honey and meat.

One who is devoted to the deity should worship with the Matsyādimocaka and recite this supreme armor (*kavaca*) with supreme devotion: *Oṃ hrīṃ*, may Caṇḍī protect my head; *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ* me... May the three-syllabled Viśvamātṛkā, *oṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*, protect my forehead;
may the Goddess Māyā always protect my two eyebrows, *oṃ aiṃ hsauṃ*.
May Viśvasundarī protect my eyes, *oṃ hrīṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ hsauṃ*.
Aiṃ Sauḥ! May [the goddess] protect my nose; īṃ uṃ ūṃ, may Māhīnī protect my two ears; ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ hsauḥ, may she protect my cheeks and eyes;
aiṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ, may Śrī Bhagā, whose form is auspicious, always pervade my mouth.

Ṇī aṃ aḥ oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ; may Bhagārūpiṇī protect my throat. Kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ aiṃ hsauḥ; may Tripurīśvarī protect my shoulders. Ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ hsauḥ; may she protect my chest. Ca... [and so forth].

May Vaidyavīśvarī—JHAṂ ÑAṂ ṬAṂ ṬHAṂ HSAUṂ AIṂ KRĪṂ HUṂ—protect my soul and the interior of my eyes; may Bhīruṇḍā—ḌAṂ ḌHAṂ ṆAṂ TAṂ HSAUṂ—protect me always; and may Hrīṃ protect my belly—THAṂ DAṂ DHAṂ NAṂ.
Śrīṃ parāvara paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ śrīṃ hsauḥ—may Mṛḍānī always protect my sides. Maṃ yaṃ raṃ śrīṃ hsauḥ laṃ vaṃ—may Kanyākā protect my navel. Śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ—may she always protect me.

Oṃ caṃ paṃ pṛ: 42a) May Guhyā and Guhyakeśvarī protect my secret parts; may Laṃ kṣaḥ always protect my private organ; may Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Liṅganivāsinī protect it; Oṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ protect my penis; may Vāriṇī protect my back. Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Huṃ.
*Huṃ pātu ūrū me pātu māṃsadā.* Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ vāṃ;
may Vātpālī always protect my shanks. Oṃ śrīṃ sauḥ klīṃ; may Kulasundarī always protect my knees. Oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hruṃ...
OṂ ŚRĪṂ HRĪṂ KLĪṂ NNAṂ HSAUḤ may protect my throat; KRĪṂ HRĪṂ HSAUḤ may protect my knee; OṂ PRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ may protect my feet; HSAUḤ HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ KRĪṂ may protect my loathsome [limbs].

KRŪVARĪCAGULPHAU AIṂ ŚRĪṂ may protect me; OṂ ŚRĪṂ HRĪṂ KLĪṂ NNAṂ HSAUḤ may protect my neck; KRĪṂ HRĪṂ HSAUḤ may protect my thigh; OṂ PRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ may protect my feet; HSAUḤ HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ KRĪṂ may protect my loathsome [limbs] of mine.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kuṭilā hrīṃ krīṃ! May she protect the soles of my feet. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ krīṃ! May she protect the bones of the feet as well as the toes.
Aiṃ klīṃ Raktakuṃbheśvarī! May Cakrūrcarī protect my semen and feces. Pā.
Oṃ śrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ hsauḥ—may you always protect me from the feet up to the navel; krīṃ śrīṃ—may Vāruṇī always protect me from the head down to the feet; klīṃ śrīṃ—may Kṛti protect me.
May Brāhmī protect me from above, and Śāmbhavī from below;
may Durgā protect me in the east, and Vārāhī in the abode of Śiva; and may Kulakāminī protect me in the north—Hrīṃ Krīṃ Huṃ Śrīṃ! Nā!

Rasiṃhī hsauḥ, may she protect me always in the northwest; Oṃ śrīṃ krīṃ aiṃ, may Kaumārī protect me always in the west; Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, may Mātaṅgī, the bringer of auspiciousness, protect me in the southwest. Oṃ.
Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, may Bhadrakālī always protect me from the south.
Oṃ śrīṃ aiṃ, may Ugratārā always protect me from the southeast. Oṃ vāṃ hrīṃ, may Dakṣiṇakālikā protect me in the ten directions. Sa.

May Tripurasundarī protect [me] at all times; may she be my refuge during pestilence, famine, affliction, and the fear of yoginīs. Oṃ hrīṃ oṃ caṃ paṃ pṛ0 43a) śrīṃ—may the three-syllabled Caṇḍī of fierce prowess protect me. Thus [ends] this.
O Maheśvarī, this meritorious armor, named *Trailokyavijaya*, which contains a mantra difficult to find in the three worlds,
is such that by its grace I am the creator of the Bhairavas in the three worlds.
O Pārvatī, by reciting this *Ṛtācar-tācara*, one who possesses a pure mind should write it on birch bark with saffron using an appropriate seat;
he shall paralyze all the gods, delude all subjects, and slay them.
One may subdue enemies by means of *kalā*; even a deity may be brought under control.
Holding [the mantra] on the arm, one may engage in battle; having conquered the enemies, one shall return home.
It is used for boats, battles, marriages, during the affliction of disease, and at times of planetary distress and the like.

One should recite this and proceed with equanimity toward all. If a man worships Caṇḍī without knowing this armor (*kavaca*), his worship will not be accepted even in hundreds of millions of years. Thus, O Goddess, is this mantra-armor.

O Pārvatī, this *garbha* (womb/essence), worshipped by the gods, must not be spoken of to just anyone; it should not be told to one who is not a disciple. Within one month, even the success of a deity that is difficult to attain shall be achieved for a mortal who recites it for three months.
"One shall attain the vision of the Lord. Thus ends the Navārṇava-kavaca from the Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra.
Now the Thousand Names are being proclaimed. The Illustrious Goddess said:
"Oṃ! O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, granter of fearlessness to your devotees;
formerly, when I bowed before you on Kailāsa, a boon was granted by you."
"Out of supreme compassion, be able to grant me my state of helplessness.
Śrī Bhairava said: "O Pārvatī, what you have spoken is true; choose a boon, and whatever you desire in your mind for the sake of perfection, I shall bestow it upon you."

The venerable Goddess, desiring [to hear this], said: "O God, tell me truly the thousands of names of Caṇḍikā that have been proclaimed. Oṃ Caṇḍī Pañcama! Pray, speak them to me with devotion, so that your grace may be upon me. Thus spoke Śrī Īśvara.

O Great Goddess, I shall truly proclaim the thousands of names of Caṇḍī, which grant boons according to one's desires to men in the Kali age; however, O Thousand-eyed One, this should not be given to one who is not a devotee. Listen to me.
I shall now declare the names of her who is renowned as Caṇḍī, the supreme mother of the three worlds; these names are difficult to obtain within the three realms,
and they cannot be protected by even the best of practitioners without a daily offering and this hymn.
In times of famine, fear of enemies, or during death and the rites of immobilization (*stambhana*),
one should recite the Thousand Names of the Goddess; then, even without perfumes, unbroken rice grains, flowers, incense, lamps, or offerings, success will be attained immediately.
The practitioner must protect this Thousand Names of Caṇḍī;
O Goddess, what I have spoken is the truth, for there is no loss of accomplishment otherwise.

For this mantra, the sages are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; the meters are Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, and Anuṣṭubh; the deities are the illustrious Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Sarasvatī; [the purpose is] dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.

The application for the recitation of the *Arthacaṇḍī-nāma-sahasra*: Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ; one should proclaim these names—Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Sarasvatī—as the seed-syllables (*bīja*) before Caṇḍikā.
Afterwards, I shall describe the great and wondrous [mantra] of Caṇḍikā; the practitioner who recites it will quickly attain the supreme vision of the piercing [of reality].
Now, the names: O Caṇḍikā, you are Mahācaṇḍā, and you are named Caṇḍā.
The leader of the Ḍas, born of Caṇḍa, fierce and more fierce than the fierce, the protectress of the Kālīs, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, who dwells in the Supreme Brahman,
the ornament of the three worlds, the secret one, the means to liberation.
O *apratārikā*, you who are not to be concealed, the object of meditation for the power (*śakti*) of Śambhu;

O *oṃ-caṃ-paṃ* (p. 45a), you who are to be meditated upon as the stainless one (*nirañjanā*), may you become the ocean-like embodiment of the knowledge of the *māyā-tattva*. You are the bestower of boons, the desired goal of those seeking liberation (*tāraka*).
She who follows the lineage of the Rishis, who possesses all human goals, who desires the Dharma, who accomplishes the purpose, who is supernatural power (ṛddhi), perfection (siddhi),
the supreme form, the skillful one, the unconquered, the envy-free, the one with the rosary, modesty, fame, and light.
O Mother, you who have become eternal through the splendor of your ancient form; O Goddess, irreproachable in the three worlds, most excellent bestower of boons;
O Mārkaṇḍeya, you who grant the fruit [of liberation]; you who are the pure attainment of the perfection of dharma, sacred knowledge, and wisdom.
Malānanā, Adṛśyā, Arundhatī, Dhanyā, Ariṣṭā, Śyāmā, Asitā, Rasā, Prakṛti, Mahatī, Jyoti, Dharmakāmārthasādhakā, Gaṇamātā, Ambikā, Puṇyā, and Vāgdevī.
She who moves through speech, whose body is speech, the excellent voice,

the beloved of the Lord of Speech (Vāgīśa), the one who fulfills desires, the one who is moistened by the nectar of bliss, she who is slow and steady, the lotus of desire, nourishment, contentment, peace, and wisdom.
She whose speech moves through space, who bestows the enjoyments of Bhogāvatī, who frequents both the enjoyed and the unenjoyed, who is skilled in the practice of enjoyment,
who consists of compassion that never falls away from the enjoyed, and who is merciful toward those with devotion.

She who is compassionate toward those dwelling on the earth protected by Indra; she who dispels the meaning of what has been understood; she who is difficult to perceive and superior in the removal of afflictions; she who is the enchantress; she who is the illusion of Viṣṇu;
she who arises from pure Māyā; she who is the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) and the Great Conquest (Mahājiti).
She who withers the seeds of the Hvarakta demon, who is intoxicated by battle and fond of war, who carries Dhūmralocana, who is the slayer of the Asura Andhaka,
who fells the one named Viḍāla, and who is the crusher of Niśumbha and Śumbha.
She is the crusher of the demon Mahiṣa, the slayer of the demon Andhaka,
the one who strikes down the one named Viḍāla, the bearer of the unassailable [weapon],
the fierce one among the fierce, the destroyer of sin, and the warder-off of Jarāsaṃdha.
Oṃ Caṃ Paṃ (Pṛ. 46a): Durmukhā, Mukhamoṭikā, your mother Devamātā, Sarvāṇī who shines with ten million suns, Rudrāṇī, Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā, she who dwells in blue silk garments, Rathinī, Pūtanā, and Senā.

She who consists of the Ṛg-veda mantras, she who is the three Vedas (Trayī), she who is perfected in the performance of sacrificial rites, she who is the success of the sacrifice, she who protects the sacrifice through song, she who is born from sacrifice, she who is the mother of sacrifice,
she who is the essence of sacrifice, she who is skilled in sacrifice, she who is dear to sacrifice, she who is the destroyer of sacrificial obstacles, and she who exists for the sake of sacrifice.

She who has knowledge as her ultimate resort, whose seed is sacrifice, who milks out the sacrifice, who is the essence of the Vedas, the presiding deity, the essence of dharma, the essence of action, the essence of wisdom,
the sovereign of sound, holding a lute, a bow, and a goad, she who destroys evil from afar.
She who holds a sword, a banner, an arrow, and a staff; she who possesses eyes like lotuses; she who holds a water-pot in her hand; she who destroys all misfortunes;
she who holds a water-pot in her hand and destroys all misfortunes.

She is the great festival of the Jñānamudrā, Yogamudrā, and Mahāmudrā; she is the thousand-eyed one, the thousand-eyed lady, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the crusher of the thunderbolt, the one with thunderbolt-limbs, the one with thunderbolt-hands, and the sovereign of the destroyer of the three cities.
She of great power, the eye of the world, the daughter of Vinatā, the Supreme Sovereign;

the Great Lakṣmī, the Siddha-Lakṣmī, who is to be served by all and yields great fruit; she whose great roar has the form of a cloud, Bhavānī, the protector of others—be present! Saṃ... [the text ends here].
The power of the primordial essence and form, whose scope is the subject matter of the Vedanta,
is the illustrious Sarasvatī who takes refuge in the state of liberation;
she is the seed-mantra that causes the emergence of the sprout from the seed through its union with the seed.
You are the diversity of mantras, nourishment, and creation; you are the Sovereign, the bearer of great clouds, the one who brings relief, the great rain, and the great ocean.
You are the possessor of crops, the maker of crops, the one of vast form, the giver of earth, and the provider of food and drink.
Rasāpūrṇā, Abhakṣyā, Bhakṣyā, Tuṣapūrṇadā, Tāpinī, Bhadrakālī, Viśvamātā, Bahvaśrutā, Gāyatrī,
Oṃ, Caṃ, Paṃ, Pṛthivī (pṛ0), Gīta, Vāreṇyā, Gopatī, Sarasvatī, and Vāraṇasī.

You are the glory of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), the refuge of great liberation (*mahāmokṣa*); likewise, you have Viṣṇu as your mouth, you perform worship to Viṣṇu, and you move within the hair on the southern side.
You possess beautiful breasts, a waist that subdues the six enemies, and you are the earth itself, O slender-waisted one. You are the island (*dvīpa*).
The little toe is to be known as the leader of the leaders of sacrifice;
the right [toe] belongs to the lords and world-protectors, while you, O Vikīśvarī,
are born from all the gods, the sovereign composed of all the gods, belonging to Yama.
Adorned with the constellation of Rohiṇī as her elder sister, encircled by Mercury and Venus, with Mercury and Moon as her beautiful girdle, possessing the form of Saturn and Rāhu as her enemies,
and displaying prowess in sacrifice and battle— [she is] the sacrificial pit for the Brahmins and the serpents.
Adorned with a garland of human heads, armlets of serpent-skins, and a girdle of skulls, she wears anklets of serpents; her body extends throughout the universe,
and she is the enchanting Great Night who has risen like the newly emerged sun.

(P. 47b) She is crowded with many rays of light, served by millions of gods, goddesses, great goddesses, and maidens; she wears a mass of matted hair, has the crescent moon of liberation as her crest-ornament, and is the Mother of every face.
The auspicious one who brings all the worlds under her control, who possesses six limbs and causes the six limbs to flow,
who causes beings to enter the Dharma through the ears, whose mouth is the four Vedas,
who bestows thousands of branches, and who is the eighteen branches of knowledge.
Pervaded by the syllable *Bhiḥ*, she who speaks all languages, Mahāśvetā,
who holds the book of the speech of the Pāṇḍavas, the mother of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, the dispeller of the mass of defects, [the source] of the Vedic scriptures...
She is the destroyer of great sins through her laughter, the pacifier of all afflictions, the one residing in the city of the Immutable (Kūṭastha), the one who shows compassion to the ignorant,
she who abides in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, and the ashes of the enemies of the gods.

She who deluded Karī, Madhu, and Kaiṭabha; she who is the essence of splendor, the one beyond darkness (Anirā), the one who speaks with a mass of radiant energy; she who severs the bonds of saṃsāra and wards off the messengers of Yama; she who consists of all mantras.
She is the destroyer of the host of base thieves, she who delights in the honey-bees of the entire ocean of nectar, she who dispels the darkness of great delusion,
the servant of Śiva, the source of all auspiciousness, and the one who dwells within misfortune.

She who bestows initiation, eternal good fortune, and beauty; she who is praised by all and worshipped by the entire world; she who destroys all dualities; she who is the gateway to the bliss of heaven and liberation; she who grants the fulfillment of all purposes and goals; she who is the knowledge of the gods and men.
She who is the refuge of all the worlds, whose mouth is like the fire of wrath yet possesses a gentle countenance, endowed with many auspicious marks, the savior of the three realms, Tārā,
the dweller on the Malaya mountain, [and] Mandākinī before the gods.
The Mistress of the Mountain of Ānanda, who is Vyāna, is born from the feet of the Earth;
she is equal [in extent] from her head to her heels, resides in the infinite and boundless tree,
consists of the herbs and shrubs that are her body hairs, and is composed of the seven continents.

She who wanders through the seven oceans of the nurse-mother (Dhātrī), she who is fierce with the seven mountains, she who is served by the seven seers and the gods, she who is born from Sadyojāta and resides in the fifth state,
she who arose from the mind of Mādeva, and who is to be known from the east as Tatpuruṣa— [she is] in the south...
Salutations to you, the most terrible and fearsome one, who stands in the sky as the Great Goddess with five faces; salutations to you, the essence of all that is delusive,
the Ghorā, equal to the three Ghorās, you who are Aindrī, Āgneyī, Yāmyā, and Nairṛtī.
You are Ṛti, Vāruṇī, Kauvīrī,
Yavīśānī, Brāhmī, the Mistress of Pātāla, Vāstavyā, she whose form is the stars, the support of the void, and Samīriṇī— these are you.
She is surrounded by various daughters of the *asuras* and *nāgas*; she dwells in the depths of the netherworld (*pātāla*),
adorned with hundreds of hoods that blaze like flashes of lightning and are embellished with hundreds of serpent-heads.
Oṃ Caṃ Paṃ Pṛ 49a) You are the goddess Nārāyaṇī, wearing garments of bark and rags; you reside within the abode of Mount Meru, bearing the banner of the Lord of Fortune (Śambhu);
you are the essence of the body of worldly existence, consisting of all the senses and the mind. Bhī...
She who bears a hundred forms of Mavaktra, Mahāvaktra, and Avaktra;

she whose head is black, whose head is great, whose head is terrible, and who has a noble face; she whose face is fire, whose face is the moon, who possesses the speed of the wind, who is of great strength, and who is difficult to overcome.
With eyes blazing like a bear, possessing the splendor of the midday sun,
fragrant, terrifying, and carrying streams of nectar; always holding various objects in her hands and intent upon seizing all the planetary spirits, she is accompanied by song and instrumental music.
She whose essence consists of flavors, objects of knowledge, passion, song, and sound; she who is the heroine among dancers, the dance itself, and the aesthetic sentiments of drama;
she who is variegated by the composition of musical performances and the playing of dice; she who is the deity who grants all desires.
Gdhātrī, Sāmasvadānasāmagā, Sumudrārambhaśā, Bhāryā, Saṃdhyālopā, Turaṃjinī, Vāmanī, Staṃbhinī, Kūrmā, Mṛtyu, Māyābhayāpahā, and Bhīṣaṇā. (pṛ0 49ba)
She is the bringer of destruction to those lords of the Dānavas;
she is the bestower of fearlessness upon all worlds, the ancestors, and men at all times.
She is protection, purification, the slayer of Rākṣasas, as well as the delighter and the moistener. [She is] the maiden...
Vīsurā, Devībhīmā, Devīcarauravā, Śākaṃbharī, Mahāśvetā, Dhūmrā, Dhūmrārkaketanā, Vīrabhadrā, Subhadrā,
Sārudradevā, Avinismṛtā, and Kapālaha.

She who possesses the staff of the trident (stākhaṭvāṅgī), who removes the fear of all worlds, who is of great splendor, who is the supreme bliss, who bestows the liberation of yoga, who is auspicious, who destroys the net of sins,
who is the source of joy, and who bears the Liṅga.
The form of the Kottara-kalā, acquired through supramundane qualities,
the great means for all accomplishments, situated within the Suṣumṇā as the sun, Oṃ Caṃ Paṃ Pṛ 50a), she who is known as the light for the welfare of the three worlds, the destroyer of enemies.
Śinī, whose abode is made of the lotus of *svadhā*, whose eyes blaze with *svadhā*,

who pacifies diseases of the head through *svadhā*, who originates from the utterance of *svadhā*, who is the field for all the realms of existence (*dhātu*), and who destroys all malevolent incantations.
She is of great majesty, adorned with the victory-drums of the Vaiṣṇavas;
she is the shower of wealth, the earth, the Vedas, and the God of gods;
she is the uprooter of the teeth of Death and the warder-off of all calamities.
She who is victorious in all battles, who humbles all enemies,
the source of all sovereignty, and the sole bestower of gifts upon the entire world;
she whose limbs are fierce yet pure and radiant, the giver of the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇiman*.
You are the form of Hāma-Īśvarī, the great accomplishment, the one of great fruit;
you are Yogīśvarī, the Mother of Yoga, perfected in yoga, the Yoginī born of the Kula, the support of the Kula, the Kaulikī, and the leader of the Kula.
(p. 50b) What is she who sports as both *khecarī* and *bhūcarī*, whose mind is fixed on the cowherd of the Gaṅgā, who yields the fruit of great knowledge, who brings about the lineage of peace,
who is called the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*), and who is pure?
The noble-minded one, arisen from all the worlds, the giver of all happiness, the destroyer of evil beings, accessible through devotion, the object of enjoyment in worldly existence,
the sovereign of the earth, the pacifier of the suffering of devotees, and the one to be served who possesses supreme sovereignty.

You are the bestower [of boons], the one with longing, the lotus-born, the one who has crossed beyond the face of delusion; you are the female elephant, the intoxicated female elephant, the lioness, and the tigress;
you are initiation, sleep, hope, and the fierce Tārā.
Śinī, Reṇukā, Raṇavaittālī, Vinatā, Kuṇḍatā, Pinī, Kātyāyinī, Devadūtī,
Śivadūtī, Vāyavī, Kumudālolanī, Lolā, Subhadrā, and Auṣadhī.
Likewise, having arisen from the sound of the syllable *huṃ*, she is Kālāgnirudravā;

she is marked with *oṃ caṃ paṃ* (pṛ0 51a); she has the directions as her garment, she is both clothed and unclothed, she is the form of all, she is the destroyer of all fuel, she is Lipipicchā, Vidārī, Cārakā, and the remover of sin.
Śinī, Piśācī, Mahāvaitālī, and Surāmāṃsavali— fond of offerings of wine and meat, dancers in Rudra’s frantic dance, possessing radiant and outstretched splendor—
are surrounded by Bhairava, who is greedy for the royal dharma as his garment.
She who has the form of the end-maker (Death) appearing as a lion trusted by the great forest fire;
she who is *sāttvikī*, *rājasī*, and *vāmā*; she who is like the darkness at the end of a kalpa;
she whose history encompasses the sun at the end of a kalpa; and she who is immersed in both water and land.

Dinī, rich with thousands of nets and counter-nets, whose nature is like the fire at the end of an eon; she who destroys those struck by the fall of the thunderbolt, who possesses the pride of a lordly elephant, who wears a garland of skulls, Kālī, Karālī, and Akṣumālinī.
Nī, Caṇḍālī, Rudracaṇḍā, Caṇḍabheruṇḍā, Muṇḍakuṇḍalā, Kālikā, Gaganalekhā, Suvajrā, Vajrayoginī, Muṇḍavipinīvāsā, Jayā, Puṣpavaśā, and Svarākṣo.
She who brings all enemies under her control, terrifying all scriptures;
she who is radiant like the sun, possessing earrings as vast as the solar orb;
she whose banner is smoke-colored and whose limbs emit great flames, raining down fire.
Vaitālī, Vajravaitālī, Māhavaitālavodhinī, Nigaḍabaṃdhasphoṭinī, Caphaṇipāśavimocinī,
Mahārāvavirūpākṣī, Śaṅkhī, and Puṣpadhvajā.

The beloved one, holding a conch, trident, and mace in her hands, the Noble One who grants the attainment of desired goals, the inspirer of enthusiasm, Splendor, the Abode of Virtues, the Supreme Goddess, the embodiment of the moon, the world of the moon, and the one anointed with lunar fragrance.
Furthermore, she is the source of the world’s bliss, possessing the qualities of a wish-fulfilling gem;
she is the one who brings about the welfare of the three worlds,
who is praised by the three worlds, who is beautiful throughout the three worlds, who is the Fortune of the three worlds, and who is worshipped by the gods of the three worlds.

Oṃ Caṃ Paṃ Pṛ (52a): Victorious one! Goddess Trailokyasundarī, destroyer of suffering and bad dreams, pacifier of grief and sorrow, bestower of the fruit of subduing the wicked, maker of good dreams for all, and destroyer of all [evil] intentions.
She who pacifies the terrible burning of fire, who removes the fear of the Śiva-cakra,
who is the destroyer of lions, tigers, and diseases, who annihilates kings, fate, and fire, who brings an end to all suffering, and who removes the fear of royal delusion— [O] Yama!

She who wields the staff, who wards off the curse of Brahmā, the Great One, the Supreme, the Destroyer of enemies, who is devoted to millions of virtues, who cuts through the torment of pride, who dries up the ocean of the sannipāta fever, [the destroyer of] sin...

Her face resembles the full moon that bestows the bliss of the Rāma-mantra; she dwells in the center of the lunar orb and appears like a rain-cloud at the end of the monsoon; she is the most excellent of all, stainless, and the very embodiment of the Supreme Self—she is to be served for the sake of her virtues.

May she who is success, the giver of success, the one praised by the perfected ones (Siddhas), the supporter (Dhātrī), the one who has transcended the supporter, the one who possesses desire, the one who faints, the one who causes fainting, the subduer, the one who binds, the one who has reached the limit of self-control, the milker of the unyielding, the one difficult to overcome, and the one who is like a young deer— may she [grant me grace].

O Goddess who protects those dwelling on the shore of the ocean, who pierces through [delusion], who brings about [liberation], who is free from the cycle of birth and death, who removes the fear of death, who is the beloved of men, who is the mother of the world, who is established upon the heads of the mothers, and who is the limit of the slow-moving [senses]—protect us!
